speechtext:
Right Hon. AY. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, I would ask
the consent of the house to move the following motion which appears on the votes and proceedings of yesterday:
That on and after Saturday, the 24th of May, instant, and every day thereafter, except Sundays, until the end of the present session, the house shall meet at eleven o'clock, a.m. That in addition to the usual intermission at six o'clock, p.m., there shall also be an intermission every day from one to three o clock, pm. and that the order of business and procedure shall be the same on Saturdays as on Fridays.
May I say with reference to the motion, it is perhaps advisable that hon. members should be informed of one or two considerations of which the government has to take account, not so much in regard to bringing the proceedings of parliament to a close as with reference to arranging for the date of a general election.
I noticed in one of the morning papers the statement that there was some understanding between the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and myself as to the date at which the business of parliament should be brought to a close. AVhile I have had a number of conferences with the loader of the opposition, and all of them so far as I am concerned, most congenial, there has been no definite arrangement reached between us as to the time of the closing of parliament. I would say the same with respect to the conversations I have had with the leader of the Progressive group (Mr. Gardiner). AVhat we have agreed to is that so far as possible we would all do what we could to expedite the business of the house in the effort to bring its proceedings to a conclusion as speedily as possible. A great deal of business has been put through within the last few days and there is, I think, every indication that hon. members are disposed to proceed with matters as rapidly as circumstances will justify. I am informed by the Chief Electoral Officer that under the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, sixty days or possibly fifty-nine days must elapse between the time at which the writs are issued and the date of the election. That means roughly that if we were to conclude the session at the end of the month of May the elections could not come before the end of July.

Saturday and Morning Sittings
There is another provision in the act to the effect that the elections themselves must be held on a Monday. The first Monday in August happens to be a civic holiday throughout the province of Ontario, and I imagine that for that reason there might be some exception taken to having the election on that particular day. If an election is not held on or before the 4th of August, it means that it would have to be as late as the 11th of August, or later. If hon. members feel that it is in the public interest to have the election delayed until the 11th of August or beyond, that is, of course, a matter within their own control, but my impression is that every member of the house feels that those who are present here are at this time at some disadvantage in comparison with their actual or would-be opponents, in that the field is open to the latter wherever they may happen to be, whereas we have to continue to sit here and go on with the business of parliament. That is a consideration which I suppose should not weigh in the minds of those who have to do with public business. However, it is a consideration that I think may affect to * some extent the way in which the balance of the business of the house will be transacted.
May I make this quite clear? The government has no desire to rush through any legislation, estimates or anything else. The estimates have been before parliament practically from the beginning of the session. Hon. members must know from having looked over them what particular items they feel are of a character that should be very fully discussed, which, in other words, will probably be the items of controversy. If those could be indicated to the whips, I see no reason why they should not be brought forward before any others, so that it may not be thought that the government is holding back certain items to rush them through at the last moment. Most of the items in the estimates, I think, will commend themselves to the house without discussion, but there may be some on which there should be some discussion. The most contentious estimates are usually those of the Department of Public Works. With those estimates we have already made very substantial progress. What remains are not very considerable.
That is my reason, Mr. Speaker, for bringing this motion before the house at the present time. It is with the hope that it may be possible to conclude the business of parliament next week; but if that is not possible, we will just have to go on a little longer. What I would, however, point out to hon. members 	.
is this: it will, I think, be agreed that so far as the public interest is concerned it will be best served by having the elections over as soon as possible, having regard to disturbed conditions likely to exist meanwhile and to the fact that there has to be, at the least, a campaign of sixty days, and that to all intents and purposes the campaign is on at the present time outside of parliament, as well as possibly to a very limited extent inside.

Having regard to the fact that the election must be held on a Monday, and to the further fact that there is a civic holiday in Ontario on the first Monday in August, I quite agree with the right hon. the Prime Minister, for my information is that it would be entirely out of the question to hold an election on that day, having regard to the conditions that exist in connection with that holiday. It is a question of whether or not we shall have an election on the Monday preceding the 4th of August or on some Monday subsequent to that day. That is what the position seems to be.

MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask leave of the house to move the adjournment to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance in connection with the hydro-electric development of the Soulanges section of the St. Lawrence river between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis by the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited and its various subsidiary companies, including the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company.
The government has approved of the above development by passing order in council P.C. 422, March 8, 1929, and in so doing the government has not accepted the plan for this undertaking recommended by the joint board of engineers, dated November 16, 1926.
Further, apparently the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company and the Beau-harnois Power Corporation Limited have violated and exceeded the terms and conditions imposed on them by the said order in counoil, and in so doing have committed acts which justify a demand for an explanation by the government as to whether or not there is an agreement between the government and R. O. Sweezey and his associates who own and control the said company and corporation whereby the whole of the unallocated portion of this section of the St. Lawrence river will be turned over to them for exploitation.
The government should disclose to parliament the reasons for its non-acceptance of the said recommendation of the joint board of engineers, and the government should further disclose to parliament whether or not there is an agreement as above indicated between it and R. 0. Sweezey and his associates, and if there is no such agreement the government should take such action as in the premises is proper and requisite.

Mr. Speaker, the subject matter which I desire to discuss this afternoon is of very great importance to the people of Canada. It is not only important to the eastern section, but to the whole Dominion. In the first instance, it will be my purpose to give the history of this undertaking from the beginning. Inasmuch as probably members have not had an opportunity of giving very much serious consideration to this important question, I believe that such a history would be very valuable to them in this connection. After I have done that it will be my privilege to discuss the financial terms of the various organizations comprised in the parent company to show very clearly how the capitalization of these companies has been such that it is not in the public interest in any way whatsoever.
Dealing with the history of this corporation, it might be said that at a certain date the Beauharnois project came under the ownership and control of what are known as the Robert heirs. It is not necessary for me to go back beyond that time, because we are not interested in the situation anterior to that particular date. The Robert heirs caused to be incorporated in 1902 what is known as the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company. We have no information as to the capital stock of this particular company or what its total assets were at that particular time. After the incorporation of the company the Robert heirs transferred to it their rights in the Beauharnois project and retained other rights for themselves. They owned, however, all the shares of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company. The Robert heirs also owned, either personally or through the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, the entire project.
The Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company had the right to divert 1,050 cubic feet of water per second. However, there developed a dispute between the company and the Dominion government over those rights, and finally it was settled in 1910 by an agreement between the company and the Dominion government, which was amplified by order in council, by which the rights of the company were definitely dealt with.
Eventually the company applied to the Dominion government to divert 40,000 cubic feet of water per second. The Dominion government secured the reports of various engineers in connection with this application,
(Mr. Speaker.]
among which was the report of Henry Hol-gate, dated May 16, 1916. The Dominion government refused to make the grant. However, in 1927, Mr. R. O. Sweezey purchased from the Robert heirs the entire Beauharnois project for himself personally. This was established by Mr. Sweezey when he gave evidence in Montreal in connection with a lawsuit between himself and the Transportation and Power Company of Montreal. During the trial the following questions were put to Mr. Sweezey and were answered by him:
Q.	Did you buy any rights from the Robert heirs within that year, that is, the year from April 28, 1927?
A. Yes. I am just trying to think of the elate. It was in 1927 I bought from Robert's. It was within the twelve months from April 28, 1926.	y
Q. And you bought it personally?
A. Yes.
Q. That is, you were acting for somebody else, L suppose, but you bought in your own name?
A. I bought it personally.
Q- (By the court) Your answer as I understand it, is that in 1927, within a year from April, 1926, you purchased the Robert interests m this scheme?
A. Yes.
So that as a result of what I have stated to the house we have Mr. Sweezey owning the entire Beauharnois project which he purchased from the Robert heirs in the spring of 1927. The price that Mr. Sweezey paid for this is not known, but a reasonably accurate idea will be given later.
During the hearing of the case of R. O. Sweezey and the Transportation and Power Company, a letter signed by R. O. Sweezey was placed in evidence and I propose to read it. I trust hon. members will follow my reading of this letter very carefully because of the fact that there are many very important implications in it. This is' the letter:
J. Alderic Raymond, Esq.,
Windsor Hotel,
Montreal.
136 St. James Street, Montreal.
14th October, 1926.
Dear Mr. Raymond,-
Further to our conversation regarding the St. Lawrence power project, in which we are both interested, I may say that though I have been familiar with this situation for some twelve years, it is only during the past twelve months that I have devoted some serious attention to the study of the economic possibilities of this one million horse-power development, near the city of Montreal, and on deep water navigation in the St. Lawrence.
Briefly stated, the power site is comprised in the natural fall of eighty-three feet, in the distance of some fourteen miles, between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis. It is proposed to divert by a canal through a clay section of level country on the south shore a minimum of
75,000	cubic feet per second on St. Lawrence

*water, or a possible maximum of 150,000 c.f.s. The effective working head would be seventy-five feet. In case of maximum diversion and 70 per cent load factor, a development of
1,350,000	h.p. is possible, and at a cost which competent authorities place at not over $100 per h.p.	_
To place ourselves in possession of all the rights essential to this undertaking, we should pursue the following course:-
1.	Acquire the Robert rights which are fundamental in regard to an initial grant which he holds to divert 40,000 c.f.s. He also holds rights granted by charter to expropriate for the proposed canal route. Numerous other incidental rights are included in his holdings which he is anxious to sell, though he wishes to participate partially in the organization svndicate.
2.	Acquire the control of the St. Lawrence Waterways & Power Company stock, which is available to us, and upon which we have already a substantial hold.
3.	Enlist with our syndicate two or three individuals, who in addition to providing some cash as their fair share, can assist us in getting our rights extended or enlarged so as to develop the entire available flow of the St. Lawrence at this point. As the whole situation is entirely within the province of Quebec, our influence has to be exerted only in Canadian political circles-that is at Ottawa and at Quebec.
4.	It will probably be advisable to enlist the participation of certain United States interests, who for their capital and initiative can be relied upon to absorb some of the power in Quebec province in connection with some powerusing industry-similar to the Aluminum Company of Canada.
The promise to use a substantial block of power in Quebec province will facilitate our negotiations with Quebec authorities, and further facilitate our exporting of power to the province of Ontario.
5.	The cash to be raised for the early stages of this project for the sole purpose of acquiring and enlarging rights to the extent of 150,000 h.p. diversion will approximate some six or seven hundred thousand dollars. It may take three or four years then before actual development starts.
In connection with personnel of syndicate, I have in mind the individuals we should enlist with us, and although I have been in touch with United States people showing a desire to join. I have hesitated to accept any one definitely until certain that each and every one is persona grata to all others.
I have said nothing about the vision necessary to an appreciation of such a project from an economic standpoint, nor have I touched upon the huge profits that may be expected, as these are matters that the ordinary business man can well picture for himself. I do not wish to minimize, however, the task that presents itself in rounding up and launching such a scheme. The actual raising of the money becomes easy, however, once the physical properties and rights have been gathered in.
Yours sincerely,
R.	O. Sweezey.
Hon. members will note two very important points in this letter. The first one is that they expect tremendous profits by securing control of this company, and also by securing 2419-151
certain rights either from Quebec, from the Dominion government or from both. It is stated very definitely in this letter that while it is essential that certain persons who have some cash should be in the organization, it is abosolutely essential that there be some people in the organization with political influence.
As soon as Mr. Sweezey assumed control of the Beauharnois Light, Heat & Power Company he advised an application to be made by the company to the legislature of the province of Quebec for the right to divert 40,000 cubic feet of water per second from lake St. Francis. This application was granted subject to the approval of the plans by the Dominion government. A lease between the province of Quebec and the Beauharnois Light, Heat & Power Company was entered into to give effect to the granting of the above mentioned application. Application was also made by the company to the Dominion government for the approval of those plans. The company, in depositing its application, submitted the following as a basis for an agreement with the Dominion government:
(a)	When making its initial installation, the company will construct its power canal to such plans and specifications and will operate its power development in such a manner that the canal when completed will conform to the navigation standards as set out in paragraph 111 of the main report, and paragraph 13 of appendix C of the report made by the International Joint Board of Engineers 1926-27.
(b)	The capital amount properly chargeable to navigation, in this connection as calculated by the International Joint Board of Engineers will be approximately sixteen million dollars ($16,000,000) and will be paid by the company. The company will also install such remedial works as may be necessary to avoid injury to existing power developments and will maintain the level of lake St. Francis at such elevation as may be required for navigation.
(c)	At any time that the government may demand, and after three years' notice, the company undertakes to install in connection with its power canal, such locks and other necessary works as may be required to make the power canal available for through navigation for vessels of a size and draught as large as any vessels which will be able to use the _ new Welland canal upon its completion, provided:
I.	That concurrently with the installation of such locks the company shall have the right to enlarge its canal and to divert through it and utilize for the development of power all the flow of the St. Lawrence river between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis with the exception of water required for floatage through the existing Soulanges canal, and with the exception of that quantity of water to the user of which existing power plants are now legally entitled.
II.	That the cost of such locks and other improvements to be borne by the company shall not exceed eighteen million dollars ($18,000,000).
III.	That in any event the company shall not be obliged to install such locks and other works above referred to until such time as will enable

the company to complete such installation concurrently with the final completion of the remainder of the St. Lawrence deep waterway.
Very strong protests were entered against this proposal. So strong were they that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) thought it wise to hold a hearing, and the company sent in an amended application. The amended application is altogether different from the first one. We must remember, however, that it was the intention of the company in the first place to secure if possible the whole flow of the St. Lawrence river. I am going to read the amended application for the information of hon. members.

January 15, 1929.
The application of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company now pending before the governor in council is purely and simply for the approval of plans for hydraulic development which will be subject to a condition that not more than 40,000 cubic feet per second shall be diverted from the river-from lake St. Francis, to be returned to lake St. Louis and used for power purposes by the company between these two points; and any condition that the government may exact, in any wording satisfactory to the government, involving that limitation, is accepted in advance by the applicant. If the engineers think that the plans should be altered to meet this declaration the company will submit to any such alteration.
Plans and specifications of the company were finally approved, and order in council PC. 422 was passed on March 8, 1929, confirming the approval. It will be noted that approval was granted subject to not more than 40,000 cubic feet of water per second being diverted from lake St. Francis. The order in council recites other conditions, but they are too numerous to discuss at this moment.
When the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company had secured approval of its plans to develop this work, a new company was formed, namely, the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited. The solicitors who incorporated this company was Messrs. Mc-Giverin, Haydon and Ebbs, of Ottawa. The Haydon referred to in this company is now Senator Haydon of Ottawa, and so far as the records on file in the Department of the Secretary of State show, this company was formed of the office staff of the above law firm, and thus constituted it entered into certain agreements all of which are set out in the statement in lieu of prospectus which was filed with the department on September 30, 1929. In paragraph 1 of this statement we find the following information with refer-
[Mr. Gardinar.l
ence to the construction of the share capital of the company:
Five management preferred shares without nominal or par value;
1,799,995 class A common shares without nominal or par value;
3,200,000	class B non-voting common shares, without nominal or par value.
Provided, however, that the said shares without any nominal or par value may be issued for such consideration as may from time to time be fixed by resolution of the board of directors of the company, not exceeding in the aggregate the sum of $50,000,000, or such greater amount as the directors may deem expedient and as shall be authorized from time to time by the Secretary of State of Canada.
In addition to the above the company entered into an agreement to isue $30,000,000 worth of thirty year, 6 per cent collateral trust sinking fund bonds of the company. At this time it must be remembered that the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited had no assets whatsoever. The company now having been formed, they were ready to proceed to do business. In the meantime, however, from the date on which Mr. Sweezey had acquired the assets of the Robert heirs in the Beauharnois undertaking, he had manipulated affairs in such a way that when the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited wanted to purchase these assets, they were owned by what was known as the Beauharnois syndicate. The members of this syndicate are not known, but I submit that in the public interest they should be disclosed to parliament. The Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited, after its incorporation and organization,^ then purchased from the Beauharnois syndicate the Beauharnois project which previously had been purchased by Mr. Sweezey from the Robert heirs. The details of these transactions are contained in paragraph 6 of the statement in lieu of prospectus.
In the first place the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited assumed the liabilities of the Beauharnois syndicate, and amongst these liabilities was a liability by the Beau-hamois syndicate to the Robert heirs. This liability no doubt arose, through the sale by the Robert heirs of the Beauharnois project to Mr. Sweezey, who formed the Beauharnois syndicate which took over the agreement with the Robert heirs to pay the purchase price provided in the agreement. The syndicate apparently did not pay this purchase price, but in conveying their rights to the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited they provided that this purchase price should be assumed by the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited. The liability therefore assumed in respect to the Robert heirs was a liability to pay them the sum of $20,000 cash

Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Gardiner
and to issue to them 21,000 fully paid up class A shares of the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited. This, then will give some idea of the real price of the Beauharnois project when Mr. Sweezey purchased it, and using this as a basis for computation we can realize how the property increased in value from the time Mr. Sweezey purchased it until it was subsequently acquired by the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited.
In addition to assuming the above liability, the Beauharnois corporation agreed to pay the Beauharnois syndicate, which was Mr. Sweezey and his friends, $4,750,000 in cash; to assume all their liabilities, and to pay them the sum of $10,000 in cash to wind up the affairs of the syndicate. On the other hand, the Beauharnois syndicate agreed to buy 1,000,000 class A common shares of the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited at $1 per share, and to pay for the same at the time the syndicate received the above mentioned sum of $4,750,000 in cash from the company. Valuing Class A common shares at the value, placed upon them by Robert Dodd and Company, investment bankers, of $60 per share, we find the Beauharnois syndicate getting class A common stock worth $60,000,000, and $3,760,000 net in cash from the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited for selling to them the Beauharnois undertaking which I have already mentioned as consisting of the rights and assets of the Robert heirs, which previously had been acquired by Mr. Sweezey.
This value of $60 per share is indicated in a comprehensive and analytical study of the values of the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited by these investment bankers in the Financial Post of Toronto, which sets forth the value of the securities of the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited. I remember right opposite me in the very seat which is at present occupied by that tribune of the common people from Saskatchewan, the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young), there sat last year another tribune of the common people, this time from Quebec. When we were then discussing a subject of this kind, that man, turning to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), said: "It would be a blessing to the people of Canada if the Prime Minister would show the gate to some of the gentlemen who compose the big interests, the Beauharnois crowd and all the rest of them." speechtext: Who said that?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
The hon.
member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). In emphatic terms he made reference to this question last year, at the very time that the negotiations in respect of the application of the Beauharnois people were taking place. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) has placed before the house a picture of a colossal financial structure built up on one of the most valuable natural resources of the people of Canada, bult up only by virtue of rights granted the company by the Dominion government under order in council. We have in that structure an example, not only of financial brigandage in its extreme, but of the old situation of interlocking directorates to which reference has been made in past years. On looking at the board of directors of the company, I find the following names:
Hon. W. L. McDougald, M.D., president of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.
I think he is a senator.
R. O. Sweezey, Esq., president of Newman, Sweezey and Company, Limited.
This company has apparently profited immensely in the financial transactions of the Beauharnois corporation to date.
A. F. White, Esq., vice-president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce.
Aime Geoffrion, Esq., K.C., director of the Canada Life Assurance Company.
Mr. Geoffrion is one of Sir Herbert Holt's able counsellors.
J. H. Gundy. Esq., president of Wood, Gundy and Company Limited.
Where have we heard that name before, even in the house? Gundy is Holt's partner in many of his firms.
G. H. Montgomery, Esq., K. C., director of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power, Consolidated.
I will speak of him a little more later. This company is another Holt concern.
S.	Godin, junior, Esq., director of British Columbia Power Corporation, Limited.
He was formerly a secretary to Sir Herbert Holt.
Miller Lash, Esq., K.C., president of the Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company, Limited.
Hon. P. J. Paradis, director of Quebec Power Company.
M, W. Wilson, Esq., general manager of the Royal Bank of Canada.
Holt, by the way, is president of the Royal Bank of Canada. Thus we observe a board of directors unquestionably "Holt" in character, and yet in it are the necessary political influences, the necessary financial influences to
2 3w>
COMMONS
Beauhamois Corporation-Mr. Garland
which Mr. Sweezey referred in his letter to the brother of Senator Raymond, Mr. Alderie Raymond, which letter was quoted by the hon. member who preceded me.
There was associated with this company in the earlier stages of its activities a gentleman named Jones. Jones, I understand, was president of the Canada Cement Company. He was a rather famous gentleman at one time and possibly still is. In the newspaper despatches last fall, the public learned that Mr. Jones had departed out of this country and had taken with him, it is alleged, the sum of $3,500,000. Search as we may, we can find nowhere any record of any service that Mr. Jones rendered the company to justify the payment of this $3,500,000. It would be immensely interesting to know to what purpose that amount of money was put. What has happened to it? Above all, what has happened to Mr. Jones? He has, so far as I am informed, not been seen in Canada since. I do not know where he has gone, but my information is that he is not in Canada at the present time and he has not been here since this transaction took place.
Thus you have the plan: first, acquisition of property as cheaply as possible; second, the creation of a gigantic capital structure for the purpose of exploiting the public, and third, the securing of the necessary political influence to bring political pressure to bear in the matter. The structure pictured by my predecessor in this debate, the obvious intention to create a gigantic public steal in connection with the matter, constitute justification for the conclusion of the hon. member for Acadia that the incorporation of this company should be cancelled. Is there a precedent for this? I find one in the case of the Long Sault Development Company, a United States concern which commenced operations and spent, it is stated, more than $1,500,000. Their charter was cancelled for reasons given subsequently by the state of New York from the government of which they had secured their charter. Amongst the grounds for the attack on the company was that it was overcapitalized. This, of course, was not the only ground upon which cancellation was granted, but it was one of them. In the proceedings in connection with the cancellation of this charter an examination of some witnesses took place. One witness, a Mr. Freeman, was examined. The examination appears in the report of the Commission of Conservation of Canada, 1913, which I have under my hand and at pages 83 to 84 the testimony of this gentleman will be found. The statement is made:
IMr. E. J. Garland.}
You cannot finance a water-power project of this kind in a locality like that without putting in various other elements and speculative elements in the way of common stock and preferred stock and brokerage and percentages to the underwriting syndicate.
Then follows the examination:
Mr. Littlefield: Do you mean to say that you do not think you could handle this proposition without the familiar process of overcapitalization, and watering of stock?
Mr. Freeman: I do not know that it is overcapitalization.
Mr. Littlefield:	Some people think it is!
The issuing of stock without anything but the expectation or the hope of successful speculation. Is that right?
Mr. Freeman:	Yes.
Mr. Littlefield:	Instead of its being watering of stock, it is issuing stock on the hope of a successful speculation ?
Mr. Freeman:	Capitalized hope?
Speculation by corporations upon the hopes and desires of the unwary and deliberately deceived public is not an unfamiliar practice in modem financial and commercial business.
It is interesting to learn that this new corporation, getting great rights from the Dominion government, is carrying out true to form this now time-honoured principle of exploitation. The question for us to decide is this: Is parliament going to sanction a speculative enterprise of this gigantic form of financial brigandage? "Capitalized hope"? What a tragic mockery! Here you have the Beauhamois Power Company with 500,000 horse-power, and with the expectation that they are going to ge't the balance, or 2,000,000 horse-power in all; and capitalizing the expectation of getting the 2,000,000 horse-power, they aTe selling to the innocent public of Canada stocks and bonds based upon their intention to acquire that 2,000,000 horse-power. There again is one further reason for the cancellation of the charter of incorporation of this company.
I now come to a new stage in this discussion-to the plan to acquire the whole flow of the St. Lawrence river. The members of the house must have been staggered by the financial picture which has been placed before them by the hon. member for Acadia, and they can now hardly be in a position to receive without absolutely falling over mentally the suggestion that it is the deliberate intention of the corporation to secure the entire flow of the St. Lawrence river at this section and to put that flow through an artificial river. Do the members of the house want t'he proof?
I have the proof for them. I turn to the report of the engineers, Mr. Frederick W. Brown, asisted by Mr. W. S. Lee and T. H. Hogg. Their firkt report was made in 1927, and from that I shall make just a few quota-

Beauhamois Corporation-Mr. Garland
tions. I have pages of extracts from it, every single extract supporting the contention that the intention of the corporation in 1927 was to get the whole flow of the river. On page 1 of the engineers' report we find this:
The initial installation is designed for the use of a daily average flow of 40,000 cubic feet per second, and the designs provide for the ultimate extension of the power development and navigation provisions, so that finally the whole flow of the St. Lawrence river could be used through the proposed power canal (or, rather, at that stage, the artificial river).
On page 7 of the same report we find this:
Later when the proposed waterway is enlarged, from time to time as required, additional remedial works could be placed in the river and the existing interests compensated, and finally the whole flow of the river could be diverted through the new artificial channel.
At page 8 we find:
The new waterway should therefore be designed for an ultimate peak flow in excess of
200,000	cubic feet per second.
A flow of 200,000 cubic feet per second takes approximately the whole flow of the St. Lawrence at that section of the river. I have pages and pages of quotations from the report of 1927 substantiating that contention, but there is no need to weary the house with them.
Now I come to a further report made by Mr. Brown, the engineer, in 1928. He not only confirms the statements made in the 1927 report, but in a letter introducing the report I find the following:
Briefly I conclude that the project as outlined in my previous report can be extended so that finally the whole flow of the St. Lawrence river could be used through the proposed power canal, and, if lake Ontario be regulated as proposed, the ultimate installation might be about 2,000,000 horse-power for commercial use including spare equipment.
The report itself contains paragraphs on pages 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7, all confirming that statement. On page 13 there is a summary of the conclusions of Mr. Brown, in the course of which he says:
If the whole flow of the St. Lawrence were used there the proposed waterway-
Indicating the intention to do it. Then in paragraph 2 I find:
Additions can be made to the proposed initial use of water by enlarging the waterway and power plant.
In paragraph 3-but there is no need to weary the house further. So much up to the year 1928.
Now I come to the year 1929, the fatal year, the year in which these valuable resources were alienated definitely from the people of Canada, In the year 1929 these interests appeared before the government of this country
and applied for certain rights. In their original application they used these words: That concurrently with the installation of such locks the company shall have the right to enlarge its canal and to divert through it and utilize for the development of power all the flow of the St. Lawrence river between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis with the exception of water required for flotage through the existing Soulanges canal, and with the exception of that quantity of water to the user of which existing power plants are now legally entitled.
In their first application to the government they ask for all of the river, but owing to the pressure of various interests, international as well as national in character, owing to the magnificent case made out by many others, this tremendous steal was for the moment stopped. The applicants had to amend then application, and the order in council which was finally agreed to reads as follows:
The application of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company now pending before the governor in Council is purely and simply for the approval of plans for hydraulic development which will be subject to a condition that not more than 40,000 cubic feet per second shall be diverted from the river.
That is a clear indication that the interests, and there were many of them-municipalities all over the province of Ontario, interests in the United States of America, navigation and marine associations, our own people in Canada -all were opposed to this Beauharnois scheme and they registered their opposition to it. In fact, almost everybody that I can think of made a protest. Then what happened? The application is reduced to 40,000 cubic feet per second. That is all that the government granted, a flow of 40,000 cubic feet per second.
By the way, there appeared before the private bills committee of the Quebec legislature a gentleman named Montgomery, to whom I have already made reference. At that time this gentleman represented some interests in Montreal who were definitely opposed to this scheme, and in the course of his statement on February 29, 1928, before the private bills committee of the legislative assembly of the province of Quebec, Mr. Montgomery, K.C., said:
Last year when we came down here there was not even a plan before the house; the idea was to grab the rights.
I submit that the promoters of the scheme have only modified to some slight degree their plans in order to meet the opposition, and they have succeeded in grabbing everything that they require. My evidence in support of that is contained first in the statement to which my hon. friend from Acadia has referred. I have in my hand an analytical study of the Beauharnois Power Company
2	COMMONS
Beauhamois Corporation-Mr. Garland
prepared by Robert Dodd and Company, the first paragraph of which reads:
In a review of the hydro-electric power situation in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec upon which we have been engaged for the last six months, the data secured has warranted our implicit belief in the inherent possibilities of great market increment being assured for the securities of the Beauharnois Power Corporation, with its prospective 2,000,000 horsepower development on the St. Lawrence river.
They can only develop 2,000,000 horse power if they get the whole flow. If they get those rights, whether from this government or the Quebec government matters not, if they get the rights to move that water through the canal, they get the entire flow of the river.
As I said earlier, I find that in making their offerings of securities to the public they are deliberately and maliciously deceiving the public unless another contingency, to which I will refer later, arises. They say:
It will be observed that our analysis discusses in circumstantial detail the expectations of this 30-year bond- share-warrant investment over a five-year period, when 1,000,000 horsepower should be in operation; and we show with that production unit, which is 50 per cent of the final objective, an earning power equal to slightly over $4 a share on the combined common stock outstanding.
I find in that same analytical study other clauses concerning additional capital reductions, another reference in column 2, and a third on the second last page, all of them confirming the foregoing. My time is limited and so I cannot quote them all. I find confirmation of these statements in the statement in the Financial Post. I pass that over. I find it in an excellent editorial on St. Lawrence power costs which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of Tuesday, January 14, 1930. The editorial was evidently inspired by the presence of Mr. Sweezey in the city or by a speech which he made. This is the first paragraph:
An interesting suggestion was made by Mr. horman Sweezey, president of the Beauharnois Power Company, in the speech he made last week	
The combined plans enable the company to develop 500,000 horse-power at reasonably low capital cost and if, at a subsequent date, the company should be authorized to use the whole flow of the river, as is likely, the capital cost per horse-power will become extraordinarily low.
I have referred so far only to an editorial and to some analytical studies, the latter, it is true, made by a responsible financial house of some standing in this country. That is not enough, and I am not satisfied to base my case on evidence of that character. Therefore I intend to go further. I take the pros-
pectus of the Dominion Securities Corporation, Limited. It is true they are allies of this general outfit. The Dominion Securities Corporation, Limited and Newman, Sweezes' & Company, Limited, are the two companies that secured this tremendous and very profitable transfer of $30,000,000 bonds and 770.000 class A stock for $27,000,000-a pretty nice deal for anybody. I have another prospectus by A. Iselin and Company, connected with the Dominion Securities Corporation and Wood, Gundy and Company. I have a third prospectus issued by Wood, Gundy and Company themselves. Mr. Gundy is a director of the concern. The Dominion Securities Corporation are directly interested in the concern. All of them put out the following statement in their respective prospectuses:
It is estimated that the unallocated balance of about 100,000 cubic feet per second, if passed through the company's canal would permit installation of approximately 1,000,000 additional horse-power. The company's proposed development, m the opinion of its engineers, is the most efficient method of utilizing the entire drop ill this section of the river. In view of the above, provision is made in the plans and considerable work is now being done -with a view to installing further units if additional water becomes available.
This is contained in the prospectuses. But what is it? It is a letter three foolscap pages in size, headed "Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited, Montreal," and is dated December 2. 1929. Why, the ink was hardly dry on the order in council passed only a few months previously when this letter appears and becomes part of their bond-selling campaign. It is addressed to Newman, Sweezey & Company, Limited, The Dominion Securities Corporation, Limited, and Wood, Gundy & Company Limited, and it is signed by R. O. Sweezey, president of the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited. Mr. R. O. Sweezey takes responsibility for saying: first, that work is now being done-and second, that the plans have been altered with a view to putting through the canal more than the amount of water they secured the right to put through from the Dominion government and the legislative assembly of Quebec-much more. The entire flow of the river is their obvious intention.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I ask this question: Is it believable that these firms with their reputation built up in this country for a fair measure of truth and honesty in dealing, men whose future will depend on the integrity of their actions, the truth of their statements, and not only the truth of their statements but the truth of the implications in their state-

Beauharnois Corporation-
-Mr. Garland
ments-is it conceivable that these men would be guilty of deliberate misrepresentation amounting to fraud? To me it seems inconceivable. I can hardly credit that the Dominion Securities Corporation, A. Iselin & Company, Robert Dodd & Company and several others-I need not bother to specify them-I cannot conceive that these great financial houses would be guilty of this deliberate fraud, for it is nothing short of that if there is no truth in the expectation of securing the entire flow of the river. So I ask this question of the Prime Minister of Canada: Is there an agreement secret or otherwise? The right hon. gentleman need not answer at the moment because my time is limited.

make a full statement of the actual financial structure. I have now shown the intention of the Beauharnois Power Corporation to secure the whole flow of the river; Both political parties repudiate any agreement in connection with the matter; I have shown that in the absence of agreement there is deliberate misrepresentation of the situation in respect of this company. I demand definite action by the Department of Justice.
I come now to the next stage. By the way, it is interesting to note that these gentlemen have overlooked nothing. Not content with the steal they are prepared to make by misrepresentation-I must assume it is that now- not content with the steal they are preparing to make by virtue of the overcapitalization with its watered stock, they are going further, and hon. gentlemen will be astounded by the story. It will be necessary, you see, to transmit the power from the buss bar to the industrial plants in different parts of the country, and so they have organized a transmission company to take care of that- not for the purpose, I assume, of losing money. They have also organized a construction company. What for? I pressume to build the canal. How are they going to get the money for the construction of the canal? By the issue of bonds. Who is going to pay for the canal? The public. It is all very easy. The next stage is to have a land company. Why? Because real estate values in the vicinity of the canal will likely advance if they have control of the water power. They want to get industries there, and they are asking them to come there now. They will have control of the Beauharnois townsite; they will have control of this place and that place, and they expect to be able to make very considerable accretions to their real estate value. They have established a land company to handle that part of the project, and to buy more land on a speculative basis. The final subsidiary company interested in this enormous octopus is a railway company. I do not know what that railway company will do, but there you have them all. These are all based upon the parent body incorporated under Dominion charter, and it may be that bonds issued by all these concerns may become prior rights on
2394	COMMONS
Beauhamois Corporation-Mr. Garland
the earnings of the bonds of the first corporation. I do not wish to deal at length with that part of the question because my time is running to its close. Let me revert however to the letter written by Mr. Sweezey. In part, he said:
In view of the above, provision is made in the plans-
Note that, that provision is made in the plans.
[DOT]-for the diversion of the entire flow of the river.
But we learn from the Dominion government, through its Minister of Public Works, that only 40,000 cubic feet per second can be used, and we learn that in the lease granted by the legislative assembly of Quebec only
40,000	cubic feet can be used. Yet we find this man coming out and saying definitely in a public letter that the plans have been altered to make it possible to secure control of the whole flow. In view of this deliberate violation of the order in council, and of the spirit and letter of the order in council, I ask that it be rescinded by the prime minister, and I think I am making a fair request. That is not the only violation in respect to the plans; we are told in the same letter that considerable work is being done and money is being spent with a view to taking the whole of the river and producing 2,000,000 horse power. The fact that it is in the future makes no difference; the principle is at stake. Either the order in council must be rigidly adhered to both in letter and in spirit, or that order in council must be rescinded. On behalf of the people of this country I ask that this order in council now be definitely rescinded; and if any legal grounds can be found for cancellation of the charter of incorporation I ask that it be revoked. To my mind this is one of the most appalling steals that has ever taken place in Canada.
I have one further reason for my stand- the effect upon the whole of the St. Lawrence scheme. In 1926 a joint board of engineers issued a report which I have in my hand. The board consisted of six engineers, three of whom were appointed by the United States and three by Canada. They went into every possible detail as to the construction of a great St. Lawrence waterway, and after their deliberations they made their report. I refer particularly to the report as it affects the Sou-langes section, and which is contained in pages 35 to 38. The main report is embodied in the opening chapter, and the appendices carry other detailed information and refer to other representations which have been made.
I find in this report that the engineers con-
sidered a plan which is equivalent to the Beau-harnois project, and they pushed it to one side; they did not favour such a plan, but they favoured the choice of two others. They favoured either the development of the Sou-langes canal section or further river development. On page 36, at section 162 of the report, I find this paragraph:
162.	Improvement of the river for navigation and power, Soulanges section: The board finds that it is practicable and advantageous to combine the improvement for navigation in this section with the development of power on a progressive program of construction of power plants, only the first part of the power development being undertaken in conjunction with the works required to carry navigation through the section.
163.	In brief, this plan provides for a dam at the head of the Cedars rapids-
The report goes on for several sections, but I shall not worry the house by reading the detailed description of the project. That project is not the Beauhamois project, it is not the one on the south side of the river. Then at page 38 I find that three proposals were made:
. (a) A lateral canal on the south side of the river

This is similar to the Beauhamois plan. Then under section (b) there is mention of a lateral canal on the north side of the river, and in section (c) there is a proposed river improvement. Under the heading "conclusions" I find the following:
The board unites in the view that the navigation improvement combined with the progressive development of power (paragraphs 162 to 169) hereinbefore set forth better provides for the present and future development of the waterway than any scheme for navigation alone, and is therefore a desirable scheme, if arrangements are made whereby power interests bear a fair proportion of the cost of the initial expenditure required.
I might explain that paragraphs 162 to 169 inclusive refer to the plan for the north side of the river.
In section 176 we find a statement which may at some future time prove to be the chief excuse for departure from the unanimous report which I have just read. Section 176 is as follows:
If it be found impossible to arrange for such cooperation in meeting the initial cost, a majority of the Canadian section-
I would ask hon. members to note the expression "a majority of the Canadian section." That would mean two out of three. The section goes on to say:
-favour the construction of the lateral canal on the south side of the river.
Only two out of three Canadians, and two out of six engineers, which is the total number

Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Elliott
of engineers on the joint board of engineers. The evidence is that the government of this country departed from the definite unanimous recommendation of the joint board of engineers. They alienated to a group of private individuals whose story has already been related the Dominion rights in regard to this section. I can say further that the Brown engineering reports, both the one of 1927 and the one of 1928 upon which the application to the Dominion government is based, embodied within their pages many paragraphs which reflected an inability to arrive at definite conclusions in many important matters. I could quote for an hour paragraphs that would say in effect:
While this equation and the levels to be derived from it may not be absolutely correct for the range of levels for which the first remedial works were designed, and while it is possible that beyond these levels it may not be accurate, it is moderately certain that for the present case it is as accurate as can reasonably be expected.
All through the report there is vagueness and uncertainty. On the other hand, we have the report of the joint board of engineers, which is definite and conclusive. There should never have been alienation of a single section of this river. It is a great international waterway and nothing should have been done until the plans were completed for the entire development and until they had been agreed upon by the governments and the interests concerned. I have come to that conclusion because this is not a river in the same sense as the Ottawa river or the Peace river; it is an international stream. I am not a lawyer, but I doubt very much whether the Navigable Waters Protection Act can apply with the same force and effect in reference to the St. Lawrence river. It is more than a river; it is a great international boundary line of waterways. Other countries have rights on the river; we are tied up by two treaties in this connection with the United States. I am informed that France still retains certain rights and that Great Britain has certain rights. The St. Lawrence might be called the jugular vein of Canada, stretching from the sea to the middle of the continent, and the waterway scheme is now being jeopardized by the alienation to private interests of these Dominion rights. I make this statement because the joint board of engineers recommended that power should be used in helping with construction in the canalization. The government have alienated a part of the section without providing for the other sections, and have definitely jeopardized the scheme. A second reason, as I said before, is that they have definitely departed from the plan of the joint international board.
Now it will take me just about one minute to sum up. First, I find that there has been gross over-capitalization of this company by greedy, calculating, cold-blooded promoters, who stop at nothing, not even the exercise of political influence, as stated in Sweezey's own letter to J. Alderic Raymond. I find further that he is guilty of statements to the public in a letter, which is public, that would lead us to conclude that he has violated the terms and spirit of the order in council. I find that there is deliberate misrepresentation amounting to fraud in the prospectuses issued by his associates in their different companies; by Gundy, one of the directors; by Sweezey, president of the corporation and one of the interested gentlemen in Norman Sweezey and Company, and so on. Finally, I find that this alienation jeopardizes the whole future of the St. Lawrence.
For these reasons and others, Mr. Speaker, which I could enumerate if time permitted, I ask that the government now rescind the order in council and, if legal provision can be made, cancel the incorporation of the Beauharnois corporation.

The Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, incorporated under a charter from the province of Quebec, made an application to the province of Quebec for a lease, which application was granted. I should like just to direct my hon. friends' attention to the terms of that lease. That was a lease of '*'the rights of the province of Quebec to such part of the hydraulic powers of the St. Lawrence river that could be developed between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis through a diversion canal on the right (southern) shore, having a maximum flow capacity of 40,000 cubic feet per second." The province reserved the ownership and the free disposition of the surplus. That was a lease of "the rights of the province of Quebec," not the rights of the Dominion of Canada, and since my hon. friend has studied carefully the order in council which was passed and which was tabled in this house the day it was passed, namely March 8, 1929, he will see that the order in council makes it perfectly clear that the permission to divert the water applies only to such rights to that water as are owned by the province of Quebec. That is the first point.
They come to the department with a lease from the province of Quebec of fights of the province of Quebec to divert certain water, which must belong to the province of Quebec under that lease. They propose to divert it in a certain way, and under the Navigable Waters Protection Act the duty of the department is to look at the plans under which that diversion is proposed and say whether or not they affect navigation. It is not a question of property rights but a question of navigation of the particular stream in which these waters flow. That was the position when they came to the department.
Notice of the application was advertised at length, and as it was a matter of special importance a hearing was given to which all 
the interested parties were invited to come and make their representations. The representations made at that hearing were, in most cases, not representations objecting to the granting of the approval of these plans, but were largely arguments from another company, which afterwards put in an application saying that if they were given approval of a somewhat similar scheme they would put in the locks as well as dig the canal. subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: May I suggest that there were also objections presented by international bodies, by marine associations, by navigators and by others. I have all the files in the matter, and I know there were many more than those two or three companies specifically interested.

I think my hon. friend

That was the main objection, and it was made perfectly clear to the applicants on that occasion that an application for the whole flow of the river would not be granted. They presented an amended application, asking for only the 40,000 cubic feet per second as the total amount to which they should be entitled.
That is the proposition which was passed upon by the department under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Section 4 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act reads:
hio work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unleg the site thereof has been approved of by the governor in council, nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council.
I appreciate the fact that no criticism has been offered as to the conditions imposed. Every precaution was taken, but we were passing only upon rights which the province of Quebec had the right to give to the applicants. The order in council and the contract based upon that order in council provide that if at any time it is found that any waters sought to be diverted by this scheme do not belong to the province of Quebec but belong to the Dominion, then the approval does not

Beauliarnois Corporation-Mr. Elliott
have effect. There is a right to cancel the approval and to take over any works which have been constructed thereunder.
What my hon. friend has said with reference to the finding of the joint board of engineers is not quite accurate. Section 22b of that report reads:	.
In the Soulanges section (second division), the board recommends a scheme for navigation correlated with a progressive development of power instead of a side canal for navigation only.
Section 176, which my hon. friend quoted, reads as follows:
If it be found impossible to arrange for such [DOT]cooperation in meeting the initial cost, a majority of the Canadian section favour the construction of the lateral canal on the south side of the river (Melocheville-Hungry bay project) which is the least expensive means of providing navigation.
A lease had been granted by the province [DOT]of Quebec and the lessees came to the department asking for approval of the plans under which the waters covered by that lease were to be diverted. It was considered to be a matter of urgency, and there was taken into consideration the fact that the water to be diverted was not in the right of the Dominion, but rather in the right of the province of Quebec. The charter and lease had been granted by the province of Quebec. The question was whether or not the diversion proposed might affect navigation, and the Department of Public Works were called upon to consider that question. The department said in effect: Navigation will not be prejudiced, injured or detrimentally affected by diverting 40,000 cubic feet per second of water in a canal, providing the canal is of a certain type. Those familiar with the evidence know that at that section navigation is very *difficult, and the type of canal which the Department of Public Works said must be constructed in order to divert the water was declared to be a canal 27 feet deep, 800 feet wide at the top and 600 feet wide at the bottom. The department said to the applicants, " If you divert that water through a canal of that type and give to the Dominion of Canada the use for all time of that canal, then it will approve your plan and not otherwise."
I do not know that it is necessary for me to -go into the financial aspect of this situation; I think that has changed entirely since approval was given on March 8, 1929. I will state quite frankly that I was not familiar with the individuals who constituted the corporation at the time application was made, nor am I familiar with the present personnel of that corporation. This matter was considered on its merit and with the greatest
possible care, and we were called upon to pass upon an engineering proposition in which the best other engineers available, along with the engineers of the department, advised that not only would navigation not be prejudiced by this water being diverted in a canal of the dimensions provided for, but that we would have better navigation than was possible with the river in its natural flow, as a matter of fact we would have one of the best navigation canals in the world.
The agreement provides further:
Whenever the governor in council so declares the right of public navigation within and along the proposed canal or any portion thereof to the same extent and in manner similar to that provided in the case of the new Welland ship canal shall thereafter exist and be recognized by the company.
My hon. friend was good enough to provide me with a copy of his notice, which reads:
The government has approved of the above development by passing order in council 1' V-422, March 8, 1929, and in so doing the government has not accepted the plan for this undertaking recommended by the joint board of engineers, dated November 16, 1926.
I have already answered that by saying that the majority of the Canadian section were favourable to a scheme similar to that provided for in section 176. The notice states further:
and in so doing have committed acts which justify a demand for an explanation by the government as to whether or not there is an agreement between the government and K. U. Sweezey and his associates who own and control the said company and corporation whereby the whole of the unallocated portion of this section of the St. Lawrence river will be turned over to them for exploitation.
It is unnecessary to conduct any investigation to find out whether or not such an agreement is in existence-there is no such agreement in existence and no such agreement has been applied for by the parties connected with this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have followed the argument of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) and if he will allow me I shall deal more or less categorically with the different points he has introduced before making some observations I have in mind to make. My hon. friend reads the Navigable Waters Protection Act and draws from a perusal of section 11 a conclusion that that act applies throughout to the St. Lawrence river. In other words he says, because the act expresses an exception in regard to bridges, it includes, by reason of making that very exception, the right to deal with the St. Lawrence river in every other particular. I do not follow the minister there. Of course, this act as far as it is sound, as far as it is constitutional, will have effect in the St. Lawrence. No one will deny that the Dominion government in connection with a harbour, for instance, or some work on the Canadian shore would, if the matter came before the governor in council, have jurisdiction to deal with it. But my hon. friend will be good enough to remember this. In stating what he did, he has missed the whole point of the argument of my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland); that is, that in respect to the national right of navigation in a boundary water that is international, the Navigable Waters Protection Act has no application. My hon. friend may say that this is not an international boundary water inasmuch as at the very spot with which we are dealing the St. Lawrence passes entirely through Canadian territory. That, to say the least, is a moot question. It was not a lawyer, but an authority whose report has been frequently quoted and whose conclusions have been generally accepted, Mr. Holgate, who made a report in 1915, and says at page
19 of that report, after reciting the treaty with the United States and other treaties in connection with this matter:
It is therefore quite clear that the St. Lawrence river is an international highway from the Great Lakes to the sea, and that neither country, following the spirit of the various treaties, could do anything to the detriment of the other country in so far as the navigation of the river is concerned.
That, I take it, is the point of my hon. friend from Bow River, and one cannot get away from that by interpreting, through the reading of one section excluding a certain thing, that the rest of the act does apply to the St. Lawrence river and that you may deal with it in the manner which has been under review. My hon. friends opposite have acquiesced in that position because when it came to a question of the diversion of water from the Niagara river, they did not attempt, although obstructions were placed in the stream, to say that that should be a matter under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. They very properly entered into a consideration of it through a treaty between the two countries, and therefore I say that at the least it is a moot point as to whether or not any arrangement such as was contemplated preceding the order in council or by the order in council should not have been carried through by a treaty between the United States and ourselves.
The second point I have taken is that this lease is a lease of the government of the province of Quebec. Very well. We went to the trouble in this parliament not so long ago of submitting to the Supreme Court of Canada certain questions for decision, questions which involved very definitely water powers on the navigable streams of this country and water powers arising from the construction of such works as canals upon the navigable streams of this country. That reference was quite futile. The questions were badly framed. It has always seemed to me that there should have been some foresight in the drafting of those questions, because it would be obvious to anyone reading them that there was nothing in them upon which the supreme court could give a judgment. It could in any event only take the place of the law officers of the crown with reference to them and tender advice. The judges of the supreme court said in effect that they could not make a decision in regard to any of the matters submitted to them unless a concrete case arises; that whatever they might say would be purely academic, and they did not choose to say anything of that character. But here we have a most important matter, a concrete case capable of determina-
2400	COMMONS
Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Geary
tion before the courts-the question of the right to the water. It was held in Tetreaultvs. Harbour Commissioners of Montreal that the river 'bed of the St. Lawrence in the province of Quebec was held by the crown in the right of the province. There has been nothing, of course, to say that the water itself, and what water provides, that is, the power possibilities of water, belong to the province any more than they do to the Dominion. We may have our views in that matter, but it was thought by the present government that on such an important matter the question should be submitted to the supreme court for decision. So I say that when we come to these two points, when we have a concrete case in which the question arises as to the rights of navigation in international waters which are navigable, and secondly the question as to who has the right to the water powers, they might very well have been submitted to the highest court of the realm for decision before the time came to pass upon this application. I think the government had that in mind and should have had the courage to press it to a conclusion. It is amply clear that the government had that in mind from a reading of the order in council, wherein the government goes out of its way to provide that should there be in some lawsuit arising in the future a decision adverse to the provinces all these rights should be cancelled. Having that in mind, would it not have been far better for the government to settle the question once for all, rather than let these people go on with their undertaking? If it was right, and was so decided, then they could go on about their business.
My hon. friend passed on to his next point, that the application was opposed by other interests. He wanted it made clear that the opposition arose not from people who objected to this company particularly, but objected only to its being granted more than a flow of 40,000 cubic feet per second. I should like my hon. friend to look at the order in council and the amendment just a little more carefully than apparently was done earlier. I am inclined to think that the applicants for this order in council were a little too adroit for those whom they had to meet, and I think that they have really made their original application over again, although they were pretending to make an amended application. The original application asked for the whole flow. You will remember that in 1928 we had a bill before the house asking for all those rights, but it did not get past its second reading. The company amended its application, and this is how it read:

The application of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company now pending before the governor in council is purely and simply for the approval of plans for hydraulic development which will be subject to a condition that not more than 40,000 cubic feet per second shall
be diverted from the river	 If the
engineers think that the plans should be altered to meet this declaration the company will submit to any such alteration.
You will note "now pending". The company has not applied for an order in council limiting them in all matters to plans which will provide for a diversion of nothing over
40.000	cubic feet per second. They have asked for the approval of plans which will meet their purposes, plans which can be enlarged, only reserving to themselves what they think is likely to be granted, the right at some future time to come to the governor in council and say: "Look at the money we have spent in order to develop the whole flow of the river. You have passed upon and approved our plans, and we have gone ahead and constructed the works. We are now using our
40.000	cubic feet per second and selling the power developed therefrom. Is it not fair to give us the rest of the power?" I say, Mr. Speaker, that they have laid for themselves a very firm foundation for making such a request in the future. I would like the government to recognize what they have let themselves in for. I refer to Mr. Sweezey's letter, which has already been quoted. Near the top of it he says:
The Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company has acquired under a lease from the province of Quebec extending to the year 2003 and under authorization from the governments of the Dominion of Canada and the province of Quebec water-power rights on the St. Lawrence river, twenty-five miles above Montreal.
They ars using there, without any context that limits it whatsoever, a statement which I think the government should take note of, that under authorization from this government they are proceeding to instal plants. The plans are later described as what? As looking for the installation of approximately 1,000,000 additional horsepower. This is what they say:
Provision is made in the plans and considerable work is now being done with a view to installing further units, if additional water becomes available.
I think nobody reading that would for one moment draw any other conclusion than that the promoters are authorized to develop
1,000,000 horse-power additional to the 500,000 horse-power under the authorization of the Dominion government, which authorization was given by the approval of plans which will develop more than 500,000 horse-power and can be adapted to develop 1,500,000 horsepower.

Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Geary

And they have sold their
stock on that basis.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
That is what 'the government has let itself in for. At that point I would ask the government seriously to consider whether it is not now in the position of lending itself to the schemes of these promoters. Referring for the moment to the liquor export bill, which comes to my mind, and setting aside the rather high-sounding platitudes and extraordinary expressions of fear of international trouble, there was one thing that justified that legislation-that this country should preserve its self-respect and should not be tangled up with rum runners or law breakers. That is a good principle. If that principle, then adopted by the government, was good in regard to rum runners and gentry of that sort, I submit that it is equally fitting of application to the gentlemen who are promoting this project and are taking money from the public in connection with it.
My hon. friend proceeds to state that there is no objection to the conditions. I do not now take any definite and specific objection to them, but at the time I was dissatisfied with them. However, I have not had an opportunity to examine in detail the conditions, although I think strong objection might very well be taken to some of them.
I pass now to the report of the joint commission. In the section which the minister read one thing stands out that cannot be controverted, that the spot where navigation development was to join power development should not be to the south of the river where the present Beauharnois development is. There is no question about that. The Beau-harnois proposition assumes to be a combination of power and navigation development. My hon. friend can get no comfort from what he read, for the joint board is entirely against the present location. True, the majority of the Canadian members-two out of three, but they were opposed by the other Canadian member, and all the American members-did say that if you introduced a simple navigation scheme on one side and a power scheme on another, it might be a good place for the navigation scheme to be along the lines of this Beauharnois development, while the power scheme would be carried out more advantageously further to the north.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I am quite satisfied my
