speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the whole
canal policy of this country has been upset by this particular contract. In 1854 the people of Canada took over the canals as a public undertaking, as part of the transportation system, and several hundred millions of dollars have been expended on those canals. That policy has been in existence from 1854 to the date of the passing of this contract, when along comes the present government and by this particular contract upsets all the settled canal policy of Canada. It gives this company power to build a canal, although by the agreement, which is a most improvident one, the government has to build the locks. The canal feature of the contract is just the joker in the deal. This is a power deal, purely and simply. The navigation part is a myth. It is to hot to read the whole voluminous record, but if hon. members will read it they will see that the contract is improvident. I doubt if it would pass a village council, let alone the committee of three members of the cabinet that sat on the case.
Let us take, for instance, the Borden administration in 1911 when the IVelland canal prosposition came up. What would the people of Canada have thought of the Borden administration if they had given Mackenzie and Mann power to build the Welland ship canal in exchange for the power in the said works. What would the country think of a steal like that in the Niagara district? Yet the present government has done this in Quebec with respect to the St. Lawrence. As I said last year, what this legislature needs is a chief bouncer. I see some gentlemen of this company walking through these halls to-night; these high "C" finance gentlemen are around
2406	COMMONS
Beauhamois Corporation-Mr. Church
these halls to-night. Whom can they influence, where do they get their pull, I do not know. They have changed their politics; they are all a bunch of turncoats. They are for one party to-day and for another to-morrow. They are just a lot of hungry political vultures, grabbing the water powers of the country from the people. In my humble view, no government can stand against the opposition of public opinion that, in the next election, that will be expressed in the ballot box in central Canada in regard to this particular nefarious deal once the people see the nature of it and what sacrifice of their interests now and in the future is involved, are fully appreciated by the people. It is one of the most iniquitous agreements that I have ever read.
Private capital should have been more progressive in past years in regard to the St. Lawrence. In this age of power development, little foresight is needed to realize the immense value of the water powers of the S't. Lawrence. This is a grant of millions of dollars made directly by the present government, without our consent and at the expense of the people, to this monopoly. Wait till you see the rates. Generations yet unborn will suffer in their industrial, economic and domestic life. We are mortgaging the labour of future generations on the St. Lawrence for the benefit of a few power grabbers of the public domain, and this is being done over the heads of the people's representatives in parliament.
Where democracy is landing in Canada, I do not know. Where is Liberalism, and where are the principles of so-called twentieth-century Liberalism? They have been scattered to the four winds of heaven. There is more Liberalism expressed in the speeches of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) than in those of hon. gentlemen opposite. Talk about the day of the Family Compact! In 1837 the Family Compact was as nothing to this family compact of Sweezey, Gundy and all the rest of them, limited and unlimited. They say that the Gaul of Caesar's Commentaries was divided into three parts; the gall of this man Sweezey and his crowd is so great it is incapable of division. This was the gentlman who went up to Hamilton a month ago to speak on the St. Lawrence question. He shed buckets of tears for the poor people of this country when he raised the United States bogey of an alternative all-Canadian canal. They need an alternative canal as much as half a dozen parliament buildings are required at Ottawa for the House of Commons to meet in. This Mr. Sweezey raised the American bogey regarding that 
canal, while he is really in league with Wall street and five American millionaires to grab this water-power and make millions for himself. He is building a big baronial castle on the banks of the St. Lawrence the like of which has never been seen in the old country, and from the tower of which he can gaze over the St. Lawrence and say, "I am monarch of all I survey." That is what takes place under this government, but I say that no government can last when public opinion in the central provinces of Canada asserts itself.
While I would like to have seen my good friends to my left a little more active a little while ago, I think that they have done good work in bringing this matter to the attention of the country. It may look a little political on their part just now, but it is pretty near time that the representatives of public rights and those who want to protect the water-powers of this country got into politics and asserted themselves, or soon there will be nothing left to give away. Mr. Backus grabbed off a whole principality for himself back of the Rainy river. He could not wait. The Seven Sisters falls crowd could not wait. The Winnipeg Electric could not wait. They corrupted the electors in the province of Manitoba in that iniquitous deal. Then there was the Gatineau deal, and now this Beauharnois, the worst of the whole lot. In my humble opinion there will be a rude awakening for the government when this country to-morrow awakens and is alive to the enormity of this deal. Parliament is being made to look ridiculous. We could not get five members to stand up and call for a vote on this question a little while ago.
The Prime Minister of this country is very fond of talking of five cent policies for the unemployed in this country. He did not talk in terms of five cents to the unemployed Mr. Sweezey and Mr. Gundy and all the rest of these power barons. Oh no; he converted them into multimillionaires. Five cents for the unemployed working man, and millions for the unemployed Mr. Sweezey and all the rest of them. That kind of policy might have been all right thirty years ago. It might have been all right then to turn over our water powers to private capitalists; but that policy was repudiated in Ontario long ago. The government of this country and its Beauhamois friends, Sweezey, Gundy and Company, will have the battle of their lives in their life work to alienate 'the sovereign rights of the people on the St. Lawrence. The water powers of the St. Lawrence are the property of the people. That question was fought out years ago, and it was established as a fact

that the water powers are the property of the people. There can be no quarter given to those who are departing from that basic principle. In the years to come this project is going to be an encumbrance and a drag on every man, woman and child in this country. A ransom will have to be paid by way of royalties on the capitalization of .this company, fixed at the highest possible figure; industry and labour in this country will be crippled, as well as agriculture, and our water powers will become part of a super-power trust in the United States.
I have found that objection to my newspaper bill came in part from the electrical trust in this country from some of these people interested in the development on the St. Lawrence. We should have turned these people out of the parliament buildings years ago. We should have had a chief bouncer to turn them out five or six years ago. Some time ago I put a question on the order paper asking the names of the president and directors of the Beauharnois Company, and the answer I got was, "No information." Fancy, no information as to who the party of the first part was.
The order in council was ultra vires because it interfered with the level of the water from the great lakes to the sea. This country settled its canal policy years ago. So this, Mr. Speaker, is what is called twentieth century Liberalism! To-morrow there will be a rude awakening for this so-called twentieth century Liberalism in the central provinces of Canada.
When the application of the Beauharnois people came before the government, it was heard by three ministers. There was the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott), flanked on the right by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), and on the left by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin). Objections were made by the shipping federation of Canada as to the levels of the lakes. They said that they could not navigate the channel if this canal was built. But the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would not listen to Lally McCarthy, K.C., when he showed how this canal would affect the levels of the St. Lawrence waterway.
Section 12 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act provides:
Parliament may, at any time, annul or vary any order of the governor in council made under this part.
Any action of parliament in that behalf shall not be deemed an infringement of the rights of the local authority, company or person concerned.

At page 164 of the evidence the parties are set out. At page 173 Mr. Holgate, the civil engineer admits that the remedial works may fall down. petition between rival power companies in Quebec. The battle for St. Lawrence power at Ottawa last winter looks more and more like a sham fight. And the millionaires of St. James street will wax fatter and fatter on the profits of electricity that should have been developed for the benefit of all the people. Every one is guilty of an indictable offence ana liable to five years' imprisonment who, being a promoter, director, public officer or manager of any body corporate or public company, either existing or intended to be formed, makes, circulates, or publishes, or concurs in making, circulating or publishing any prospectus, statement or account which he knows to be false m any material particular, with intent to induce persons whether ascertained or not to become shareholders or partners, or with intent to deceive or defraud the members, shareholders or creditors, or any of them, whether ascertained or not, of such body corporate or public company, or with intent to induce anv person to entrust or advance any property to such body corporate or public company, or to enter into any security for the benefit'thereof.
In Rex v. Gillespie, it was ruled that:
In considering the charge against the president of an incorporated company for publishing a false statement under code, section 414, judicial notice will be taken of the statutes of another province under which the company was incorporated, requiring the president to be chosen from the directors; and a warrant of commitment against the president, as such, after vroot , malmer of incorporation, need not allege that he was a director.
So both the province and the Dominion have jurisdiction in this respect over prospectuses. Whether the justice department will prosecute -well, you know who is running the government of this country. This government today is nothing but a government of big interests and appetites. When I see those gentlemen walking around arm in arm with the leading members on the other side of the
[Mr. Church. 1
house, I have very little hope that the interests of the people will receive much attention.
As to the engineering side of this project, the mover and the seconder of this motion have read from the report contained in the return which was brought down last session at my request. They have picked out a few of the good points in that report, but they in their time limit have touched only the fringe of the subject. There is going to be a rude awakening shortly for the government and for these interests. Some of these people are seeking financial aid across the border with their Wall street allies. I have the evidence taken before the federal trade commission of the United States which investigated the power trusts over there. This commission has control over power and gas utilities in that country. The evidence shows that those American power trusts have agents walking the floors of congress and of all the state legislatures. They have bought papers and spent millions. Our power magnates are just as busy in our legislatures. Is it any wonder that the people of this country are going to wake up when they see the Tvay their water powers are being handed over for private greed and gain? This government has not five cents for the unemployed to feed their starving women and children, but to the unemployed of the Sweezey class they hand over millions of dollars. The member for Bow River estimated that Mr. Frank Jones, who was the chief mover in getting approval of the company's plans by the federal cabinet, made 82,500,000 out of his share in the project. Well, I have been reading some of the leading financial papers of the United States and of Wall street and their writers say that he made from $4,500,000 to $6,000,000 out of the sale of his permit interests. That was what the permit from the hon. Minister of Public Works and the government was worth to Mr. Jones. A new company was formed. As the hon. member for Bow River said this afternoon they amalgamated all the subsidiary companies and the prospectus says untruthfully that they secured water rights on the St. Lawrence capable of developing 2,000,000 horsepower. If there is any concern for public rights in the Department of Justice they will see that the criminal code is enforced against those responsible for issuing the false statements contained in these many prospectuses. The Minister of Justice still allows two innocent young men of Ottawa to remain in Kingston penitentiary, even after the Attorney General of this province and the local crown attorney declared they were innocent, and a mistake made, and that they have not heard a word from the Justice department. Why

Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Woodsworth
are those innocent men allowed to languish in prison? Why treat the poor one way and the millionaires another? To-day there is a power family compact. Talk about twentieth century Liberalism! Well, the public will soon have something to say about this "twentieth century Liberalism."
The shipping federation representing those interested in the operation of ocean steamers objected to the Beauharnois plan for the reason that the project would change the levels of the river and would interfere with the flow of water to the port of Montreal. It is pretty easy to see how the departmental engineers can change their opinions. When Sir Adam Beck applied for permission to build a dam at Morrisburg these very same engineers said that it would lower the levels and interfere with the port of Montreal so seriously as to prevent the proper operation of shipping. But when they were confronted with the Beauharnois application they turned a complete somersault and said it would not affect the port of Montreal in any way. Last session I was told by my leader that I had a free hand to introduce my bill to transfer the power of approval of such projects from the minister to parliament, but unfortunately I was ill towards the end of the session and could not proceed with that measure. We made another attempt on March last but were not able to bring the question to a vote. Last year, headed by the leader of the opposition, sixty-seven voted in favour of the second reading and seventy-two against.
This contract is so obnoxious that there has been nothing like it since confederation. Today parliament is a mere cipher and we might as well go home. No matter how we may protest, the government can give away the whole of the St. Lawrence water powers to a few favourites and thus make them millionaires overnight. Is it any wonder that the people of this country are disgusted and that they are becoming alarmed at the way these water powers are being alienated to benefit a lot of millionaires? The question of federal and provincial jurisdiction over the St. Lawrence waterways was referred to the supreme court last year, but it was all a sham battle. Was the Beauharnois question referred to the supreme court? Of course not, the Sweezey company could not wait.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could have
wished that this subject had come up earlier in the session. However, much of the information that has been placed before the house
to-day has been available only in recent weeks. I know some of us may lay ourselves open to the charge of attempting to make preelection capital out of this question, but I suppose that we shall have to run that risk, for it seems to me to be of such great importance that it cannot be ignored, even though we are within a few days of prorogation.
The member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) accused some of us in this corner of the house of not being interested in public ownership. May I remind the hon. gentleman that last year within a very few days of the opening of parliament my colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) made an inquiry concerning the St. Lawrence waterway. It is recorded in Hansard of 1929, page 80, as follows :
Mr. Heaps:	Will the government, before
issuing permit or licence for the canalization or water-power development on the St. Lawrence river submit same for the consideration of the house ?
Mr. Mackenzie King:	The Navigable Waters
Protection Act provides that no works may be constructed in navigable waters unless the site has been approved by the governor in council or unless such work is constructed in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council. In the case of any application for the construction of works in the St. Lawrence river, coming within the scope of the act in question, it is the intention of the government to follow the procedure in force hitherto, as prescribed in that act.
That procedure was not at all satisfactory to those of us who believed alike in the policy of government ownership and the control by parliament of important matters of this character. For that reason, on February 25, 1929 I introduced a motion to this effect:
That in the opinion of this house no disposition of the natural resources under the control of the federal government shall be effective until ratified by parliament.
Hon. members in the house may recall that that motion precipitated a debate which lasted for a week. I do not think it can be said that we in this corner of the house have neglected to direct the attention of the country to the situation which exists. Last year in Winnipeg we lost the Seven Sisters falls; this year we have apparently lost the St. Lawrence river, and hon. members will realize that the loss of the St. Lawrence river is a much bigger thing than the mere Beauharnois development. I take it that this development meant a surrender of Dominion rights. I am not proposing to discuss the constitutional question of jurisdiction as between the Dominion and the provinces, but I say that the St. Lawrence river is in an altogether different class from the ordinary Canadian river. It is not a
2410	COMMONS
Beauhnmois C orporation-Mr. Woodsworth
provincial stream; it is not merely a Dominion stream but it is international. It is one of the important links in the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence system, and each part of t'he river should be treated as a part of the whole system. For example, the United States has treaty rights permitting free navigation. I submit to the house that power and navigation developments are inseparable, and it has been an exceedingly narrow reading of the British North America Aet which has permitted the government to turn over to one province certain valuable power rights on the St. Lawrence. This government and other governments haive not always read the British North America Act in quite such a narrow fashion. Take, for example, the Montreal harbour commission. I am told that that commission operates under the Dominion government; it maintains cold storage plants and a great variety of concerns which might conceivably be understood to be provincial in character. On Saturday the prime minister is to open formally the harbour bridge. I am only a layman and I do not pretend to understand the intricacies of the law, but if the Montreal harbour commission can build a bridge from shore to shore across the St. Lawrence river I cannot see why we should say that the development of power must of necessity be entirely provincial in character. There is very little doubt that the action taken in developing the Beauharnois system is blocking the general scheme of navigation which should involve the whole of the St. Lawrence.
Within the last few months some very interesting articles written by Mr. Harry Sifton have appeared in some of the Toronto papers. In those articles he pointed out very clearly that the power development ought to bear the cost of canalization. I do not want to argue the point, but to my mind it is obvious that his contention is correct. If we allow power to be developed in the haphazard fashion we are doing at the present time, it will be impossible later on for the Dominion government to shoulder the heavy burden of putting through the canal. The canal could be constructed at very little cost to the Dominion government.
The serious charge has been made by the members for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) and Bow River (Mr. Garland) that the government is lending itself to a colossal " grab." I do not think the expression used by the hon. gentleman is too strong. Simply by acquiescing in this kind of thing and by having passed an order in council which has been the foundation upon which these transactions have been based, the government has been lending itself to a colossal grab-unless indeed the govern-

ment should now take prompt action to cancel the agreements contained in the order in council. In my opinion the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) gave a very disappointing answer, and he took an extremely narrow and purely departmental view. He did not touch at all the charges urged by hon. members in this corner but stated that the province of Quebec had the right to grant a charter. I do not know why the hon. gentleman undertook to decide a question which has been before the courts and upon which there has been no final decision. We all know that the province of Quebec claims the right to issue charters, but as the member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) very clearly stated this afternoon, we should have had a final decision from the highest judicial body and should not have allowed the matter to be settled by order in council. The minister stated that the government had adopted the policy which the majority of the joint engineering board had advocated. I do not think that the hon. gentleman was quite ingenuous because if hon. members will read the report they will find section 162 as follows:
The board finds that it is practicable and advantageous to combine the improvement for navigation in this section with the development of power on a progressive program of construction of power plants, only the first part of the power development being undertaken in conjunction with the works required to carry navigation through the section.
It was only in case it was found impossible to carry on such cooperation that another arrangement was suggested and that the majority of the Canadian section suggested that this route would be possible for navigation purposes. I think therefore that consciously or unconsciously the minister was rather misleading when he made his statement.
I do not think we should consider this particular transaction as being of a nature distinct from other similar transactions which are taking place all over this North American continent. I have before me an issue of Labour under date of May 20, 1930. This paper is published in Washington. There is a cartoon here which shows a portly old gentleman labelled " The Power Trust " holding a sort of coffee mill labelled "The Holding Companies " and into this mill he is pouring a stream of water which flows out in a stream of gold dollars. The caption is " Turning water into gold " and the cartoon illustrates a speech made last week by Senator George W. Norris in the United States Senate. Mr. Norris said:
Chemists in the past have been working for years and years. ... to devise a method by

Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Woodsworth
which they could make gold, synthetic gold. These power trust officials have beaten the chemists to it. They have made hundreds of millions of gold out of water-nothing but water. It does not even need to be clean water; it is usually muddy, dirty water, but they are making gold out of water daily; and the consumers of light and power, the little fellow who reads his newspaper by electric light, the woman who uses electricity to wash clothes, the big manufacturer who consumes hundreds of thousands of horse-power in making things that the American people use, the miner who operates the coal mines-all of them are contributing their part to the great operation of the power trust of converting water into pure, yellow gold; and we sit idly by.
Then Senator Norris goes on bo refer to conditions in Canada, he says:
Partly as a result of the wisdom of the Canadian government-
I am afraid he should have said the wisdom of the Ontario government.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Not in all cases.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Possibly not.
Partly as a result of the wisdom of the Canadian government in its handling of power matters, the Canadian manufacturer gets his power at approximately one-half of what the American manufacturer on this side of the river has to pay for power.
And again:
In 1925, power in the United States, I mean industrial power, cost 11.5 mills per kilowatt hour. During that same year the manufacturers of Ontario, Canada, paid 6.1 mills. In 1928, it cost 13.4 mills in the United States, and only 6 mills in Ontario, or considerably less than half the cost in the United States.
That is in Ontario only, and under public ownership. Unfortunately, although we have begun so well, we are permitting the greatest water-powers in the eastern part of this country to pass into private ownership. There is the difficulty, and it is for this reason that I feel we cannot allow such a matter as this to pass unchallenged.
I think the hon. member for Bow River has shown very clearly that there has been essentially a violation of the order in council. That order in council states very clearly that only a small portion of water is to be diverted. Undoubtedly the company is making plans for the diversion of a much larger amount; they hope ultimately to get the whole river, as has been stated already. I want to read their prospectus again; I do not think it can be read too frequently or emphasized too strongly. In the prospectus signed by R. O. Sweezey, the following statement is made:
In view of the above provision is made in the plans and considerable work is now being done with a view to installing further units if additional water becomes available.
I may say also what I do not think has been pointed out already, that they are even now taking steps to secure supplies of water beyond their 40,000 cubic feet per second. In their prospectus, they say:
In addition to the above water-power rights the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company has entered into a contract with the Montreal Cotton Company providing for the acquisition of the latter's rights to divert water for power purposes from the St. Lawrence river at lake St. Francis.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the purchase by the company of the right of the Montreal Cotton Company to divert water is in itself a definance of the lease and of the order in council. In addition, it had already been represented and the fact is that 40,000 cubic feet will produce 500,000 horse-power. The statement that the Montreal Cotton Company's water combined with the company's water will produce 500,000 horse-power is not in accordance with the facts, and the truth of the matter is that both waters will produce a great deal more power than the above. In fact, in the Financial Post of February 27, 1930, it is stated that the company will be able to develop 112,000 horse-power with the Montreal Cotton Company's water, although the report of the joint board indicates that only 10,000 horse-power can be so developed. The company, therefore, is guilty of two offences in acquiring the Montreal Cotton Company's water and in advertising thus; first, a breach of the terms of its lease and of the terms and spirit of the order in council, and second, misrepresenting the facts with reference to the amount of power from the above sources.
We have had so many figures given to-day that I fancy the ordinary man is somewhat confused. I do not intend to add very many more, but I should like to ask what is the value of this colossal capitalization that has been built up. It has been estimated, according to figures given by Robert Dodd and Company, that altogether there is a capitalization of some $380,200,000; that is, when the company gets actually into operation, in the course of a few years, interest and dividends will have to be paid on that huge amount. That sum appears to be required in order to build a project which will cost the net sum of $50,000,000, and the total expenditures which have been made in acquiring a property whose value would amount to only $1,280,000.
Surely the government has a responsibility in a matter of this kind. If a boy steals a bottle of milk worth 10 cents from a door
2412	COMMONS
Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Woodsworth
step, he is sent to gaol; if some small robbery takes place in connection with any of our stores, we sometimes send young offenders to gaol for one, two or three years,, yet here are men making millions upon millions out of this country and apparently nothing is to be done about it. The Minister of Public Works simply folds his hands and says, "Well what can we do"? Surely, if the government of this country is worth anything it is here to protect the people against the big robbers as well as against the small robbers. If we have to pay interest and dividends on this huge capitalization; if we and our children after us are to be enslaved in this way, surely it is time the people realize the actual situation.
There are certain political aspects of this case which I confess I think require explanation. The letter from Mr. R. 0. Sweezey to J. Alderic Raymond has been read already, but I should like to refer to one or two sections of this letter. The first section points out the necessity of acquiring the Robert rights, and section 4 of the letter reads as follows:
It will probably be advisable to enlist the participation of certain United States interests.
I should like to know what interests have been enlisted.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: And why?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I think we ought to know why, and I think we ought to know how.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: And for how much.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
There are a number of questions which suggest themselves. I do not think that Mr. Sweezey, in starting a program of this kind, had any doubt as to how he was going to carry it through. The least this government could do is to make an investiga lion as to what United States interests are behind this concern. I am very sure that if there are no United States interests behind it at the present time, it will not be very long before that condition exists. A super-power trust exists on the other side of the line and this is extending itself in every direction. The American newspapers for the last year or so have been filled with revelations as to what is happening in regard to this matter. Before reading clause 3, I will read the preceding phrase, in order to link up. It is as follows:
To place ourselves in possession of all the rights essential to this undertaking, we should pursue the following course:
3. Enlist with our syndicate two or three individuals, who in addition to providing some cash as their fair share, can assist us in getting

our rights extended or enlarged so as to develop the entire available flow of the St. Lawrence at this point. As the whole situation is entirely within the province of Quebec, our influence has to be exerted only in Canadian political circles -that is at Ottawa and at Quebec.
How has that influence been exerted at Ottawa and at Quebec? It is quite evident that powerful interests have been exerted or the corporation would not have secured these rights. It was quite evident a year ago that powerful interests were exerted in connection with the Seven Sisters falls, both at Ottawa and at Winnipeg. I think this house is entitled to know what interests are now at work at Ottawa.
The company was incorporated with a dummy board of directors.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Who were they?

It might be worth while taking a few minutes to show just who were the provisional directors of this corporation. They were as follows:
Osmond F. Howe, barrister-at-law, Trust building, Ottawa, Ont.
Duncan K. MacTavish, barrister-at-law, Citizen building, Ottawa, Ont.
Belle Fraser, stenographer, Ottawa Electric building. Ottawa, Ont.
Lyla Brennan, stenographer, Ottawa Electric building, Ottawa, Ont.
Edythe H. O'Malley, stenographer, 115 Siparks street, Ottawa, Ont.
Bessie Conniffe, stenographer, 115 Sparks street, Ottawa, Ont..
Lillian Dell, stenographer, Trusts building, Ottawa, Ont.
Elsie M. Burritt, stenographer, Ottawa Electric building, Ottawa, Ont.
Gwen Gunderson, stenographer, Trusts building. Ottawa, Ont.
Kathleen Havey, stenographer, Ottawa Electric building. Ottawra, Ont.
M. H. Kelly, stenographer, Ottawa Electric building, Ottawa, Ont.
Those were the provisional directors of this great corporation.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Did they get anything out of it?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Of course it is not unusual to have a dummy board of directors, but the layman sometimes wonders why it is necessary. Why was it necessary for a lawyer of the standing of Mr. Geoffrion to come all the way from Montreal to have the company incorporated by Messrs. McGiverin, Haydon and Ebbs? These are questions which should be answered.
The personnel of the board of directors has already been given to the house, but I notice included in that board the name of G. H. Montgomery. It is rather curious that in opposing the application of the company made before the Quebec legislature, the report

Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Woodsworth
of the proceedings before the private bills committee at Quebec on February 29, 1923, shows Mr. Montgomery as saying:
Last year when we came down here there was not even a plan before the house, the idea was to grab the rights that had apparently been worked out in one or two of those commissions for private interests.
And so on. Shortly after Mr. Montgomery appears as one of the directors of a corporation described by him as not being in the best interests of the companies he represented or of the province. Apparently one way of getting on the directorate of a big corporation is to attack that corporation hard enough.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Better be careful.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: What have you got in your mind?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: This is not a bid for a position on the directorate. Another name appearing in that list is that of the Hon. W. L. McDougald. I think we all know the name of Senator McDougald.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: He is the power behind the throne.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
The Hon. Mr. McDougald was a member of the national advisory committee, to which the Minister of Public Works has referred. As the minister was not able to give us that information, I think it would be well to put on record the members of that committee. They were as follows:
Hon. G. P. Graham, chairman.
Thomas Ahearn, Ottawa.
Hon. W. E. Foster, St. John.
Beaudry Leman, Montreal.
Edward D. Martin, Winnipeg.
Doctor W. L. McDougald, Montreal.
Hon. Sir Clifford Sifton, K.C., Toronto. Major-General John W. Stewart, Vancouver. Hon. Adelard Turgeon, Quebec.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Does that include political influence?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. McDougald
had something to say last year regarding the St. Lawrence waterway. In speaking to the Senate on April 19, 1928, as reported at page 236 of the Senate Hansard, Mr. McDougald said:
Honourable gentlemen, I desire to make a statement on a question of privilege, and to give an absolute denial to certain newspaper implications reflecting on my honour and integrity, both as a member of this honourable body and as a private citizen.
He made reference to certain editorials which had appeared in the Toronto Globe, and continued:
I am concerned, however, only in giving an immediate, unequivocal and absolute denial to the implication of the Globe despatch that I am connected with the Beauharnois Power Company.
He may not have been connected with the Beauharnois Power Company at that time, but to-day he is one of the directors. I notice that the following appears in the prospectus sent out by Mr. Sweezey:
Management preferred shares (no par value),
3 shares.
The management preferred shares above mentioned confer on the holders the exclusive rights for a period of ten years from September 17, 1929, to elect and remove the directors of the corporation and otherwise confer in respect thereof the same rights na if each management preferred share were a class A common share. The management preferred shares at the end of the ten-year period will automatically be converted into class A common shares, but, with the consent of all the holders thereof, may be so converted prior to that time. These shares have been provided to ensure continuity of direction and policy during the important initial period covering the construction and early operation of the development of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, and will be held between Hon. W. L. McDougald, M.D.; R O. Sweezey, Esq.; and A. F. White, Esq.
We have the extraordinary spectacle of Doctor McDougald, a member of that national advisory committee, denying that he had anything to do with this corporation, and to-day he is a member of the directorate and one of three who hold these management preferred shares which give them absolute control for the next ten years.
There is just one other matter that I really should not pass by, although it may not be of great public importance, but I notice among the engineers of this new corporation, the name of Thomas H. Hogg, Esquire, of Toronto. I suppose an engineer has the right to find his work wherever he can, but a year or so ago Doctor Hogg was employed by the Manitoba government to give expert advice with regard to the desirability of handing over the Seven Sisters falls, and he then appeared as having been lent by the Hydro-electric Commission of Ontario, a public body. Now he is apparently the engineer in connection with this private concern.
I do not intend to weary the house by going into any further figures or statements in regard to this matter. I want to ask the simple question: In view of the facts that have been brought out this afternoon-and I think most of them are indisputable-what does the government propose to do? That is what we are all interested in. We are not here-at least I am not-to make definite charges, but I am here to give wider publicity to some of
2414	COMMONS
Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Woodsworth
the facts which have been before the public now for some weeks in these prospectuses and in the statements that have been issued by these investment companies. It seems to me that now that the facts are known to the public, it is for the government to act. I do not think they can evade their responsibility by simply asserting that this is a Quebec matter. It is not a Quebec matter; it is a Dominion matter. It is a Dominion matter because the order in council, without which this company could not have been organized, was passed by the Dominion government and the government has it entirely in its own power to cancel that order in council.
Only last year when some of us were urging that these properties should not pass irrevocably out of the hands of the country without parliament being asked to make a pronouncement, the Prime Minister told us that under the Navigable Waters Protection Act the power to cancel was already in the hands of the government. That power being in the hands of the government, surely we have brought sufficient evidence before the government to warrant a revocation of that order in council. Further, I would pass on the suggestion which came from the hon. member for Bow River. In a matter of as great concern as this, we ought to have an investigation by the Department of Justice. I do not mean a narrow, departmental investigation; the Department of Justice should take the initiative in making such an investigation as would convince the general public that their interests are to be safeguarded in the future and as would prevent a corporation of this kind fastening itself upon not only this generation but generations to come.
Turning water into gold! You talk about morality; you try to impress morality upon our young people throughout the country; but how are we to have either personal or national morality if a few individuals are in this way to be permitted with impunity to make their millions out of their fellow citizens?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I am as anxious as any other hon. member to see the early prorogation of parliament and an opportunity to try our fortunes at the polls. I cannot, however, let this occasion pass. I do not think I shall traverse any ground already covered in this debate, but there are two considerations which drive me to my feet.
In the first place, I do not believe the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) made a fair presentation of the case this afternoon.
I know there are within his knowledge certain facts which should have led him to say some-

thing other than he did. I took down his words, and the effect of them was that he was approached by the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company with a lease of such rights as are owned by the province of Quebec. That is one statement which, after the word " lease " will appear in Hansard to-morrow. Another was that they were dealing with water power rights which the province of Quebec have the right to grant. Then he wound up by telling the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) that he was in the wrong tribunal. He did not attempt to answer the case; in fact I would say he rather admitted it. That is one reason why I am driven to my feet. I am prepared for any change of base or front on the part of the government, but I am not going to let that change take place unless I have a chance, if I believe public honour and the interest of the people are involved, of saying that what is done is contrary to what is right, contrary to what a government should do.
Listen to this: for two weeks in October, 1928, I sat in the Supreme Court of Canada, day in and day out, as many other counsel did, I with two other counsel, representing British Columbia, the government represented by more than half a dozen counsel, and every province in Canada represented. What was the occasion? It was what was known as the waterways and water powers reference. It was action on the part of this government. They asked the Supreme Court of Canada, by answering certain questions to tell them who owned the water powers, who had the right to the property in the water of the rivers and streams of this country. Shortly stated, that is what the supreme court was asked to do. The government was represented by a number of very distinguished counsel who said over and over again-and this is in the notes which I have; I have not had an opportunity to refer to them, because I did not know until this afternoon that this debate was coming up-that they were instructed by the Attorney General for Canada-they did not say the Minister of Justice-to contend that His Majesty in the right of the Dominion held the propery in and control of all the waters in all the navigable rivers and streams of this country, and further, mark you, that the Dominion of Canada owned all the power that could be developed from those waters. Therefore, all the Beauharnois Company had or could get or has now is the property of the Dominion government.
We cannot go into the legal argument, but there is in connection with it a point that is so important I know it will be appreciated by

Beauhamois Corporation-Mr. R yen man
some. The chief point in this two weeks' session was: Is there or is there not a public right of navigation? Every province but one declared that there was not a public right of navigation. The contention of the counsel of this government was that if there was a public right of navigation then under the British North America Act, section 91, supplemented by section 92, it followed beyond any contradiction that the Dominion of Canada owned the water powers and had the property in the water in the rivers and streams of 'Canada.
The case of the provinces-I am speaking generally-was weakened by one fact. The eminent counsel for Quebec, the late Eugene Lafleur and Mr. Geoffrion, said that they could not contend that there was not a public right of navigation in the province of Quebec. Therefore, if the contention of the government's counsel was right, there was, following a public right of navigation in the province of Quebec, the ownership and control of all the water powers in the province of Quebec by the Dominion of Canada. Therefore, when the Minister of Public Works says that he was approached with a lease given by the province of Quebec, which purported to deal with these water powers, I ask him and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), when did they surrender this important ground? There was no other ground. When did they surrender this ground which took them to the supreme court asking for a decision of the court as to who was entitled to the water powers and the electrical energy developed therefrom in the Dominion of Canada? That was the whole case; there is no question about it.
As has been stated, the questions submitted to the supreme court were not answered. If the question of a public right of navigation had been admitted by all the provinces, I believe that the supreme court would have answered the questions. Those who will take the trouble to read the reasons for judgment given by the justices of the supreme court will readily see that there was much to be said on behalf of the government of the Dominion of Canada owning all the water powers that could 'be developed upon any navigable stream in this Dominion.
This order in council, Mr. Speaker, is a wonderful document. Remember, it was drawn up after this hearing before the supreme court. Its drafting is artistic; there is no doubt about that. On page 6 of the order in council, with the margical note "Reference to supreme court" it says:
That in view of the combination of the two questions of power and navigation, it was
deemed advisable to refer to the Supreme Court of Canada, a series of questions to the end of determining the respective rights of the Dominion and provincial governments in the development of power. The supreme court has recently submitted the result of its consideration of the various questions asked. The conclusions of the court do not furnish sufficient ground to establish a well defined line of action with respect to power but as the question of fully protecting navigation is the dominant issue so far as the Dominion government is concerned, it is found that favourable consideration may be given to the proposal of the Beau-harnois Light, Heat and Power Company, which, with certain modifications, may be utilized for the requirements of navigation in that stretch of the river.
There was not one counsel, Mr. Speaker, who was bold enough to get up and even murmur during all the course of that hearing that there was any claim that the navigation of navigable waters could be interfered with by any province. That is altogether aside from the question, and whoever drew up that *order in council ought to have known it. But 'it does say, as will! be noted, that there was involved the question of the ownership of power. I have forgotten just when the judgment was delivered, but the hearing was in October, 1928, and judgment was given about six weeks or two months afterwards.
What I wish to refer to next is the debate that was held in this house on February 19, 1929, when the government was asked not to pass this order in council in favour of the Beauhamois Company. One would think, after hearing that this Beauhamois power was such a valuable asset-its value was scaled up this afternoon to $308,000,000-that a government that was anxious to keep for the people of Canada all that they were entitled to would have done something to have this question of ownership settled. Beauhamois power is only one power. There are thousands in this country, all valuable. The Dominion government took care to go to the courts with counsel. A return was made as to the cost, and while I do not remember the exact figures, I am sure that the hearing cost $100,000. Add that to the $308,000,000. Remember that every province in the Dominion of Canada was represented by one or more counsel, and that two weeks were occupied in the hearing of this case. The judges could not answer the questions submitted because, they said, some of them were not properly framed. I do not suggest that they were deliberately not properly framed. It was known that this application of the Beauhir-nois Company was before the government, what would be the natural thing for any business man to do under those circumstances, where hundreds of millions o( dollars wp-.e
2416	COMMONS
Beauhamois Corporation-Mr. Ryckman
involved, and that is no exaggerated statement? Would not eare have been taken to ascertain who owned the water-powers, and who was entitled to the money that might come from their development, who was going to enjoy such a splendid property producing such magnificent services. Would that not have been the natural thing to do? But it was not done.
I come now to the 8th day of March. We find that while this matter was still in suspense and undecided, while nothing had occurred to weaken the government's case, but rather i.he opposite, while the government certainly had a case that should be decided on its merits, this important order in council was passed in favour of the Beauhamois company.
The government, Mr. Speaker, has failed in its duty, and I say that that admits of no contradiction. If this Dominion of Canada in its right as against the provinces is entitled to untold millions of property, then that question should be decided. As I said, the hearing before the supreme court took place in the month of October, 1928. No further step in relation to deciding who owns this water-power has been taken by the government now in office. It should have been taken; it must be taken. Speaking wholly for myself, I say that after this next election, of my own motion I am going to ask the leader of my party to see that the question is determined whether the Dominion of Canada, which we all represent, is entitled to this property worth millions of dollars, or whether it can be given away by those who do not own it.
In conclusion, I desire to say that I think it very strange that there is no representative Tory in this Beauhamois group. Do not imagine that it is on that score that complaint comes. They were assisted in every way. The Minister of Public Works said: We had nothing to do but to accept this lease which was made by a lessor who might not have had the power to grant it. I say, Mr. Speaker, yes, the government did have something to do. At a private sitting in with these people you gave them the land for their locks and all their appurtenant works; you made it nice and easy for them. The whole thing was on the skidway in favour of these men and against the interests of this country, and the government saw that it was done.
Let me refer to the debate which took place last session. It will foe found on page 786 of Hansard of March 8, 1929. The Minister of Public Works then said something different from what he says to-day.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this house has
been listening to what by all odds is one of the most important discussions of this session. The statements made this afternoon by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) were so lucid and the national aspect so apparent that I feel every member must regard this question no longer as one purely of local concern but one that touches the whole conduct of business in this Dominion.
I do not think observations need be lengthy. There was incorporated in the province of Quebec a company known as the Beauhamois Light, Heat and Power Company. It had the right to divert 40,000 cubic feet of water per second from the St. Lawrence river. A very distinguished engineer conceived the happy thought of developing power in the river. He wrote a letter to a friend of his and pointed out that the way in which this could be done was to secure the support of capitalists, and likewise political influence. That letter was read this afternoon. He proceeded to carry into effect his purpose and he succeeded. For those who succeed in the efforts which they honestly make I think no one has a word of condemnation. The public interest becomes important only when private enterprise touches the public in the way that light, heat and power touches them; and it becomes of transcendent importance that every step that can be taken to protect the public interest should be taken.
This government, in its executive capacity, was called upon to determine, through the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott), whether or not permission should be given to divert the water from the river and lake through a canal to another lake. A hearing was arranged and permission was granted. But before the permission was finally granted, the application was amended, and the permission was given to divert only 40,000 cubic feet of water a second , from the river through a canal which was to be constructed by the applicant company. The applicant company was the Beauhamois Light, Heat and Power Company, incorporated, as I have said, by the Quebec legislature, and under our law as it stood at that time it was essential that permission should be given by the government of Canada to enable the works to be constructed.
The province of Quebec claims to own the water over the bed of the river, it being in that province, and it bases its claim upon reasons which were presented in the reference to the Supreme Court of Canada and which 2419-153
have always been presented in that sense by the provinces, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has indicated. The Dominion of Canada, without having the question finally determined by the court of last resort, or propounding questions that in my judgment would make an answer possible, proceeded to grant the authorization. That authorization was granted upon conditions. This therefore implies that the government realized that it had the right to impose conditions upon the grant of the authorization. The conditions it did impose are set out in the order in council. That was done by the federal government acting in its executive capacity.
We thus have the Beauhamois Light, Heat and Power Company acquired by the engineer, who commenced operations as indicated, with the assistance of capitalists and politicians whose influence he thought powerful enough to aid him in carrying forward his work. That, at least, is his statement of the matter. He did not then proceed to sell the securities of that corporation; and here is where the federal parliament becomes responsible. The Secretary of State granted letters of incorporation to the Beauhamois Power Corporation Limited-not to the Beauhamois Light, Heat and Power Company Limited, that had the licence from the province of Quebec. It was not that company that sold its securities, it was the company created through the instrumentality of the Companies Act passed by this parliament. That company came into being for the purpose of acquiring the shares in the Beauhar-nois Light, Heat and Power Company Limited and its subsidiary and allied organizations. That company, the Beauhamois Power Corporation Limited, had, of course, to comply with certain provisions of the Companies Act. Hon. gentlemen read this afternoon the statement filed in lieu of prospectus by the ten students at law and lawyers in Ottawa who had no interest in the transaction and who were acting through Ottawa solicitors headed by Senator Haydon. The principal political figure in the company at present is Senator McDougald, who is chairman of the Montreal harbour commission and one of the three managers of the Power Company, according to the prospectus, for a term of ten years.
The company came into being under circumstances to which I have referred. It therefore owes its origin to a Dominion act, and the question before us at the present time is: What safeguards have we, as a parliament, imposed on behalf of the investing and consuming public with respect to this corporation

2418	COMMONS
Beauhamois Corporation-Mr. Bennett
and others of the same character? I recall a question which was being discussed when I first came to this parliament. The question before us at that time had reference not to a power company but to the question of capitalization of companies. The labourer is worthy of his hire; the engineer with courage, vision and foresight who foresees great possibilities is entitled to just compensation for his efforts. When the public subscribes money to make possible the development of a great enterprise it is very often given an interest in the common shares of the corporation in order to make the proposition sufficiently attractive to induce them to advance their money so as to carry on the undertaking. The next question is: To what extent should those who promote the undertaking and foresee its possibilities be compensated for their foresight, their knowledge and their effort? That question has not yet been answered. It is now more than fifteen years since I stated my views in the House of Commons that something should be done by parliament to indicate the extent to which the free distribution of shares to promoters should take place, and thereafter become the basis upon which rates for a public necessity such as electric current are established. There can be nothing more important; it is important in Manitoba; it is important in Alberta; it is important in British Columbia, and it is important in these great central provinces. There can be no doubt as to the right of the promoter to just compensation for his efforts. But what is just compensation; what is fair compensation; what is a just recognition of the services rendered by the promoter? Mark you, the promoter renders a distinct service; he has had vision and foresight, courage and enterprise, and it has been through his persuasive powers that others have been induced to enter into the undertaking and to provide capital so that it may flourish and develop into a great and powerful undertaking. But, there must be a limit to it, and when that limit may be controlled and is not controlled I attach the responsibility to the government. When the government of this country had the opportunity to exercise control; when they granted permission to this corporation to carry on its operations-for, mark you, it could not function for one day and could not market a kilowatt of power without approval by the government of its plans to divert water from the lakes and stream above to the lakes and stream below- it should have exercised that control. In the face of the story we heard to-day the present situation constitutes an outrageous proposition. In my professional career I have had to fMr. Bejinett.]	*
do with a great many such enterprises, and I have an idea of what would be just compensation for men who promote, foresee and have vision. When it comes to talking in terms such as we heard this afternoon, will any member of the house say that the consuming public is getting a fair deal? Is the consuming public getting a fair chance to have the rates controlled and the prices fixed for power which is absolutely essential to the development of the country? In the light of what was stated this afternoon, will any member stand in his place and say that the promoter's compensation is just when we begin to talk about a hundred million dollars? It staggers our imagination.
I must confess I had no conception that these figures ran into the millions that they do until I heard the hon. gentlemen make statements this afternoon, and I took the trouble to investigate some of those statements. I find the situation to be simply this, that the gentleman who was the president of the enterprise at the time of the application to this government is no longer the president. He retired, and at the time of his retirement it was openly stated in the public press that he offered to buy or sell, and that he sold his interest in the company for upwards of 83,500,000. He thought that the public were being asked to pay too much to the promoters. I ask the government: What steps were taken to provide for the regulation of rates; what steps were taken to provide against the overcapitalization of this enterprise? I read and re-read the conditions imposed by this government. And what conditions did the government impose: (a) for the regulation of rates; and (b) over the capitalization of the enterprise? None. And so with unrestrained activity this corporation, with the sanction of the government through the offices of the Secretary of State, with three management shares, for a period of ten years is under the control of three men, one of whom is a member of the Montreal harbour commission, and no restrictions, restraints or conditions are imposed by the government of Canada upon the exercise of powers which touch vitally the lives of hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions of people. I wonder if hon. gentlemen realise what it means when they talk about 2,000,000 horse power. Do hon. gentlemen appreciate or understand what the development of this great valley means in industrial life? It means the bulding u,p of great industries and the creating and promoting of Canadian life. This country can become one of the greatest countries on the face of the globe if we but utilise the vast resources we have at hand. I fancy,

Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Bennett
however, that there will not be a Canadian who when reading the story placed on Hansard this afternoon will not regard such action as described a menace to the industrial and economic development of Canada. I make that statement in all sincerity, because I have made it my business to look into the relation between electric power and development. I have studied it. I would ask hon. members to notice the United States across the line; take note of the power they have at Niagara, and compare that power and its possibilities of development with the possibilities which exist in Great Britain. Instead of the British industrialist being able to have an electric motor attached to every shaft in his factory as is the case in the United States, he has to depend upon steam for the development of power. In Great Britain the water power is very limited; there is practically no hydroelectric energy, and they have not yet solved the problem of cheap power as we understand it here. Within a radius of a few hundred miles of the city of Buffalo, 500,000 horse power is available. Go into the modem plant and see there the electric motor attached to every machine; with a twist of the wrist the machine stops, and with another twist it starts. There is no question but that there is a great loss of energy involved in the use of steam power. In this country we are able to utilise the great forces of nature to the maximum and in this way we can produce power cheaply.
But what position are we in? The power that once belonged to Canada and to all the people-and I have a very strong conviction when I use those words-has now passed irrevocably out of our hands. The price at which that power is to be sold for Canadian development is to be passed upon by three managers for the next ten years. That is what it means.
Let us look at this thing fairly. There are the names of the persons concerned; some of them are friends of mine. Does that deter me from the discharge of my public duty here? It does not. My public duty here is to point out just what I aim pointing out to this country, that the power development of the great natural resources of power and energy that infuse life into factories and make them efficient instruments for the purpose of making this country great, can come about only by a realization that this development must be under terms and conditions that enable such power to be available to the Canadian people on the cheapest possible terms. These resources are held by us from Providence in trust, not for the few but for all; they are held in trust for the Canadian people and not for the few. I am the last 2419-153^
man who would deny to the man with enterprise, initiative and courage just compensation for his efforts, but I ask any hon. gentleman sitting opposite, whether he be a capitalist or otherwise, to read the figures given this afternoon and say whether this country of ours has had a fair deal. We are the beneficiaries; the crown in the right of the Dominion has been the trustee; they and they only could grant the permission, and when they granted that permission did they impose a single restriction or condition that would secure to posterity and to this generation as well the use of that great natural power given to us by Providence, the extent and value of which is such that it should make Canada equal any nation in the world?
That is the question. When we talk as we have been talking about the necessity for protection and why it is necessary to put ourselves on terms of even and fair competition with those who are carrying on mass production in other countries we must remember that one of the most valuable factors, namely the great hydro-electric possibilities of Canada, is now passing out of our hands and cheap production is then rendered less and less possible. I say, sir, that while I sat in my place and listened, as I did this afternoon for the first time, to those speakers and remembered what I have read as to the prices at which securities upon the stock exchanges are being sold, I realized that in its possibilities this was one of the most gigantic enterprises this country has ever had to consider, and the question is well worthy of the consideration of parliament even if it were the day before dissolution.. I am only sorry that it should not have been considered before this. I have been recreant to my duty in that it has not been so considered, and after all I heard during this discussion this afternoon I realized that fact.
I do think, and I say it to the Prime Minister, that this matter should be the subject of judicial inquiry. It should be inquired into; there have been statements made which necessitate that procedure being adopted, why should $3,500,000 be spent for little or nothing? What is the reason for this vast financial scheme? Why, there are now several thousand shares apparently available for sale on the market at $15 per share which, in itself as you will observe, involves a vast sum of money. What is the reason for these things being done without our having some knowledge of just what Mr. Sweezey meant when he pointed out what had to be done in order to secure the results which he has attained? Why was the opinion of the engineers disregarded; why is it that to-day we

Then there is another matter. In western Canada the ramifications of this undertaking have been felt. I ask the Minister of Railways and Canals: What about the foreign press; who controls it? I ask him that question.

Of course I accept my
hon. friend's statement as to that, but apparently those near to him have seen to it that he does not know. Why the sudden change in policy in that press? Who controls it to-day? Who was sent out there by the interests in Montreal to make the transfer? Let us have that question investigated and answered also. All I can say, sir, is that while there is no opportunity here this day, in this house, to make this investigation, there will come a time when this matter will be investigated and made known to the Canadian people. That is as certain as anything in the world.
Go to the United States and watch what they are doing there. We talk about our institutions: the United States Senate lays bare everything. What are we doing in this country? We are pussyfooting about matters of this kind, because men think that your friend or my friend may be associated with this matter, and we have not the courage to stand up and talk about it. Well, sir, I value my position in public life, but I would rather be relegated to private life and be there forever than remain silent on an occasion of this kind.
That is what I have to say; let there be no misunderstanding about it. It may mean that I will be subjected to the threats of the great financial powers that are behind this venture. I snap my fingers; that is my answer, and I want the Minister of Railways to go out and investigate and answer to the people of western Canada as to who is responsible for the transfer and sale of the foreign press, so-called, in the city of Winnipeg. Let him go out there and see who is

responsible for the references made in these papers now. Bring them home. We know where they stood when the Seven Sisters matter was up. Go find where they are now. There was bound to come a time in the history of this country when we would have what they call a "show down", and now the time has come.
I confess, Mr. Speaker, when I contemplate this matter and when I regard all that is involved in it, not to thousands but to millions of people who some day will fill this great valley around the St. Lawrence, which might become one of the greatest industrial centres in America-the Ruhr of Canada; when I contemplate what those figures meant this afternoon, my feeling of resentment gets the better of me. I ask hon. gentlemen if this thing is to be tolerated. It rests with us, with each of us, to say whether or not it shall be tolerated, and I believe that in the end the common sense of the Canadian people will prevail and that, great and powerful though the promoters have been, they are .not sufficiently powerful to control the common sense of the people of Canada.

Objections were taken, but 'the questions were finally settled upon after
several conferences, the last of which was held in my own office, presided over by myself, so I must know what I am talking about. The matter before the court was not a question as to the ownership of the bed of rivers or the ownership of the ordinary water-powers on navigable rivers within a province, but dealt mostly with the ownership of power developed as a result of navigation works undertaken by the Dominion government. That question has not been settled by the court, but my hon. friend is now contending that in so far as the water-powers of Ontario and Quebec are concerned, on the St. Lawrence or on other navigable rivers, those provinces are to be placed in a position of inferiority to the other provinces of this Dominion. Are not these two central provinces entitled to their natural resources as are Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and the western provinces?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: The comparison made by the hon. Solicitor General is not a fair one; this is an international stream, not a national one.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Can we contend that the
St. Lawrence river, in so far as the Canadian 'section is concerned, is to be considered as 'international, and are we to cede our interests 'in it and say that we cannot dead with that section of the St. Lawrence without consulting the American government or the American people?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Never.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I am not in favour of
that. The Canadian section is Canadian and should be dealt with by Canadians in the interests of Canada. I will not agree with the theory advanced this afternoon by the hon. member for Toronto that because of treaties passed one hundred years ago, which gave to Americans the right of free navigation on the St. Lawrence river, we have to consult 'them when we want to deal with the Canadian 'section of our principal river.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I advanced no such theory.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I think the people of
Canada will be behind me and not behind the hon. member for Toronto in this connection.
The Beauhamois company is not the only one exploiting power in Canada-there are many others. The provinces of Ontario and Quebec claim that the water-powers within their boundaries are part of their natural resources, and the provincial governments claim the right to dispose of them. Are we

If we are going to leave to the provinces in the future as we have done in the past, the disposal of their natural resources, are we going to dictate to them whether those resources should be handled by public or by private ownership?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: That is another matter. Are we as a parliament going to tell the province of Ontario that tire public ownership is bad and that private ownership should be adopted? subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: The Quebec government has granted this lease, as it has granted other similar leases, and has adapted, whether rightly or wrongly, a policy of private ownership as being the proper way to develop power. Are we going to wipe out provincial autonomy? Canada is composed of nine provinces; there is a federal government and there are nine provincial governments-are those provincial governments to be recognized or are they as entities to be wiped out? If they are to be wiped out, very good, but if they are to be recognized, provincial autonomy has to be recognized in every branch and in every part of Canada, in the west, in the east and in the central portions.

speechtext: What would have happened had the order in council not been granted?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend has asked a very pertinent question. The rights exercised by the province of Quebec in connection with the Beauharnois company are subject to and restricted by the paramount right of Canada as to navigation. Whenever power is to be developed by a province, either through a hydro commission or through a private company, that development cannot take place unless and until the Dominion government is satisfied that the interests of navigation are protected. In the order in council [Mr Cannon.J
which was passed conditions were laid down to protect navigation on the St. Lawrence, not only for the present but in the future. We have never done anything more than that. If we are going to change the law, very well, but so long as the law remains as it is to-day, we cannot do anything more than that.
The hon. gentleman mentioned the finances of this company and spoke of fraud and fake representations. I am not here to defend that particular financial group; if they have done anything wrong, leit them be punished. However, I think every hon. member of this house knows that the administration of justice in Canada is in the hands of the attorneys general of the different provinces. If these people have committed fraud, it is for the Attorney General of Ontario or the Attorney General of Quebec to prosecute. That is another well recognized principle of constitutional administration. It is very well for the hon. gentleman to talk about a gigantic swindle; to talk about unfair rights; to talk about the public being crushed. If that were so, could the leader of the opposition explain why so astute a gentleman as Mr. Ferguson, premier of Ontario, would make a deal with those people for power for his province?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: He cannot get it anywhere else.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: If what the leader of the opposition said were true, how could Mr. Ferguson make a deal for 250,000 horsepower with this syndicate?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE

This is my last word. The leader of the opposition is more familiar with the financial world than I am, unfortunately for myself, I shall admit; but when I was listening this afternoon to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) giving the names of the financial firms which were interested in this Beauharnois issue, I said to myself: Since when have these people become dishonoured? They are the leaders of our financial world. Since when have they become thieves? Since when have they done things by reason of which tlie Canadian people should withdraw

speechtext: They do not say it and they cannot say it. They say they hope they may get it, but we have to stand by what we have done and not by what people say we might do. What we did was to protect the interests of navigation; we refused to give the complete flow of the St. Lawrence when they asked for it, and what we shall do after the election, because again we shall have the executive authority, will be to protect the interests of navigation.
